speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I am sure everyone has also realised it is too wet!

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Floods submerged our pathways and toppled our trees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of our deliverymen got stranded in shelters because it became too dangerous to ride.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our science and our senses tell us so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister Grace Fu shared last month, “With climate change, we can expect more of such erratic weather in future.” Sir, I remember learning about climate change when I was still a little boy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I was 10 years old when the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was set up in 1988.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It saddens me that my daughters Ella, Katie and Poppy will grow up facing the same environmental issues I learnt about when I was in school so many decades ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, my fellow Members of Parliament and I will present recommendations on 10 topics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The GPC for Sustainability and the Environment as well as the Young PAP have worked hard and worked together – in partnership with climate activists, business leaders and members of the public – to come up with these recommendations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are pushing hard for changes but, at the same time, we are mindful not to push people and businesses away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are mindful of the trade-offs, particularly for our economy and jobs, and we have sought to find the right balance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All of us believe that a healthy economy and a healthy planet can go hand-in-hand and should go hand-in-hand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our first point of departure is the common understanding that climate change is a global crisis that strikes at the very foundations of how Singaporeans live.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In his 2019 National Day Rally speech, Prime Minister Lee called climate change “one of the gravest challenges facing humankind.” He outlined how Singapore will be hit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rising sea levels may put coastal areas underwater.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Developers will have to build at higher levels than before.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has always managed to build our way around problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We built upwards, touching the sky with skyscrapers and HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We built outwards, reclaiming land from the sea.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We built our NEWater plants, turning waste into water.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But climate change is not an ecological threat that our engineers can just build around.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Near and far from our borders, cities and villages will face the test of climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Farms and fisheries will be reshaped, disrupting supply chains.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There may even be geopolitical conflicts over water resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, we cannot hope to escape climate change through superior engineering and high-quality design.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Globalisation means climate change will find a way to hit our livelihoods, our breadbaskets and our peace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This brings me to the second reason we have brought the Motion to this House: it upholds Singapore's reputation of fulfilling our international commitments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister Vivian will tell you, we are a little red dot, but there is nothing little about our voice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have led negotiations in the most significant multilateral agreements of our time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have hosted peace summits, had UN conventions named after us and had our people elected to lead UN agencies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All this is made possible because our diplomats at MFA and our Public Service work so hard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is also made possible because Singapore has a reputation for responding when the international community calls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, our Motion today responds to what is perhaps the most critical call of our century – former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon's call that every country must take urgent, immediate action to combat climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than anyone else, Singapore understands the significance of going together, not going alone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On these rough tides, every pair of hands counts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have signed the Paris Climate Agreement, but we must do more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our recommendations today provide specific proposals on what we can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our third and last reason for bringing this Motion here today is that it responds to voices Members of this House must all have heard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These voices come from Singaporeans, young and old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past few years we have seen them build, organise, research, educate and advocate to move the needle on climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Esther has been City Developments Limited's Chief Sustainability Officer for over 25 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It really is not common to see a business leader advocate about climate change like she does.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In one breath, she is talking about Sustainable Cities Index; in another, she is casually dropping data about Canada's climate change policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no point in just talking if you do not take action." Good thing, she also walks the talk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has worked with her company to cut emissions, secure green loans, fund green start-ups and create awareness campaigns.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has won the SDG Pioneer award, given by the UN to business leaders who have done an outstanding job advancing their Sustainable Development Goals or SDGs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Despite all her time working with titans of industry, her inspiration comes from youths.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To quote her again, from interview with The Edge: "Given their energy and desire for a bright future, youths play a vital role in helping our planet to recover from the harm humans have inflicted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to engage, encourage and empower youths to drive the green agenda and impart them with the necessary skillsets and tools to drive sustainability for decades to come." I could not agree with her more about youths being the future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken with many of them in the past few years and decades.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Xiang Tian is a young man studying at the Singapore Institute of Technology.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You may have seen him holding a microphone and giving a heartfelt speech at the Singapore Climate Rally in 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But his passion for the environment goes much further back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It started in kindergarten, when NEA gave out a Green Package to his class.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His memory is vivid: it was three books and one music CD, instructing him on how Singapore will pile up with trash if he did not reduce, reuse and recycle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He learned, as we all do, that big problems require big solutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, he started studying engineering, with an eye on finding solutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He founded LepakSG, which consolidates environmental events in a single calendar. "Lepak" means relax, but he is nothing but hard work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, what he finds energising is that the climate change community are the kind of people who, like him, are happy to volunteer their Friday nights and weekends discussing problems, researching solutions, gathering feedback, reaching out to public agencies. "No one is Superman," he told me. "We cannot save the world by ourselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we can move others and we can change systems." And that is exactly what he is doing and, as many of us know, he is doing this while infamously always wearing his slippers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like Xiang Tian, Lastrina found a connection with the environment at a young age.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her dad came from Pulau Sakijang Pelepah, or what some of you may know as Lazarus Island.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Growing up around sea captains and divers, she gained a natural appreciation for the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But almost 10 years ago, she heard what the experts were saying about climate change. "Something worrying was happening," she said.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was time to graduate from appreciating the environment to helping it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And so, in 2015, she started the Singapore Youth for Climate Action with some friends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She understands instinctively how powerless other youths feel in today's world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The solution, she says, is to shine the light on what they can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her message is one of empowerment, and Singapore is lucky to have her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For Wei-Shan from our Young PAP, or YP, sustainability has a lot to do with changing people's mindsets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Running a business that designs gifts, she found that clients would almost always opt for plastic packaging even when she recommended greener alternatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a challenge, but it is one we cannot shy away from.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is why the many public consultations organised by Wei-Shan and her passionate team mates at YP brought industry experts and climate activists to the same table.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Each party gets the chance to persuade and be persuaded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Good policy, she says, must balance the viewpoints of different groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Wei-Shan is also a mother of two young children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are used to seeing their faces during our many Zoom calls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These little ones fuel her passion for sustainability. "I want the world to be better for them in 10, 20 years’; not worse," she says.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like Wei-Shan, Cynthia's passion is informed by her work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having worked for over 10 years in the maritime sector, an industry at the heart of global business, she recalls that MNCs were working on sustainability, even before it became a buzzword in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is why she believes good climate policy must be pragmatic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, it must reduce emissions, and of course, it must ensure the welfare of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the path to that outcome should involve working with the private sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have the capacity to change, and we all benefit if we help them to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is why Cynthia and her passionate team of activists at the YP climate change policy team envision such an important role for businesses in their position papers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But business aside, climate change is, for Cynthia, about responsibility. "We have treated the Earth badly," she says.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is time we do what is right for the future generations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope Members of this House do not make the mistake of thinking any of these people work alone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Xiang Tian, Lastrina, Wei-Shan and Cynthia were all at pains to emphasise the work of others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are just four names amongst thousands in Singapore who are waging the battle against climate change in their own ways.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We may not agree with everything climate activists say or do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But let us pause and remember: these are Singaporeans who care deeply about helping and protecting something other than themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as importantly, they speak up because they believe in the capacity of this Government to listen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is that not something we should respond to?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, my fellow MPs and I will discuss 10 topics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should ensure that these higher standards are robust.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It means when we buy something, we look not just at the price tag, but also at how much it will cost us to maintain, use and dispose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This practice helps us spend less and waste less.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, Government contracts should measure and set standards for carbon footprints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is already a common practice in Europe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should mandate it, especially, for high-emissions infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, we can increase standards on accredited efficiency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, every Ministry should be required to publish a yearly Sustainability Report.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This can just be an adapted version of the confidential Resource Management Plans that they already must prepare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will tell the public how each Ministry is greening its operations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To sum up, we can do a lot by enhancing our Government's sustainability standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will also note that many of our Government's contractors also service other clients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When we tighten our sustainability requirements, it can spark process improvements across the supply chain, creating a multiplied effect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But Sir, the Government's work does not stop at its procurement or its operations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It sets policies, and this means there are a lot more things it can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My colleagues will focus on nine other topics and propose changes in policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, these proposals were formulated from over a year of public consultations with business leaders, researchers, activists and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some of the ideas were sparked by YP's Climate Change policy team.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Members' various legislative assistants also contributed to making this happen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My thanks to my own climate change team, led by Elliot.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The carbon tax is perhaps Singapore's most important policy tool against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that we needed to start low to avoid spooking investors and I agree that our economy needs to emerge from COVID-19 first.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But our 2030 target of $10 to $15 per tonne increase is far too low.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some feel that it simply will not work as a way to slash emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IMF, which has one of the most conservative models out there, says our rate needs to be no lower than S$99 in 2030 to keep climate change at safe levels.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if we decide that $99 is too high, $15 is not anywhere near enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to be honest with ourselves: without a high enough carbon tax, even with all the other things we do, our emission level might remain high – far too high.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Research studies from Ireland, Scotland and British Columbia find that a revenue-neutral carbon tax, where the money collected is poured back into the economy, could slash emissions while boosting the economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is the path we need to take.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Don Wee will share more of his thoughts on this topic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Henry Kwek will also share his views about cutting our emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second topic is professionalisation of the carbon documentation industry to heed the UN's call for global harmonisation of carbon documentation standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The third topic is embedding sustainability into our industry transformation maps (ITM) or having an ITM for the sustainability sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both of these topics flow from the reality that climate change is terrible, but the fight against it can create good jobs for Singaporeans and grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan will share her take on these two topics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fourth topic is the Green Mark scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Green Mark sets standards and certifies sustainable construction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a good idea, but its standards need to be improved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A Green Mark Silver or Green Mark Gold building, today, may not be very green at all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Poh Li San will speak on this topic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fifth topic is climate education and the sixth topic is increasing public access to emissions data of top-emitting entities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both of these topics are about empowering our citizens.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can we teach our young ones about climate change?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What can we do for them outside the classroom?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And can we release more data on carbon emissions to the public?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sustainability is an increasingly integral part of people's lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must provide the education and the data needed for people to act in line with their moral compass.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin will share more on the topic and Ms Hany Soh will also speak about community involvement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The seventh topic is charging points for electrical vehicles or EVs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore aims to phase out cars with internal combustion engines by 2040.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this shift will be hard if we do not have enough charging points for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government needs the private sector to build more charging points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to find new ways to help them do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh will speak on this topic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Gan will also speak on the eighth topic, data-sharing mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The world of business competition is a treacherous place, but robust data-sharing frameworks can help provide the trust needed for industry players to share data, become more efficient and reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is time to add climate defence as the seventh pillar to reflect how climate change is an existential threat for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Seah Kian Peng is passionate about this topic and will discuss this in his speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the 10 topics, we are all also concerned about our forests in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, the Government shared an environmental baseline study carried out by HDB to guide future plans to the Dover, or I should correct it now, Ulu Pandan Forest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I share their concerns and I too hope that the Ulu Pandan Forest and other forests like the Clementi Forest will be protected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe we can work together to find a middle ground and embrace sustainability in the development of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are our vanguard in our fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is needless to say that forests are also sites of great, irreplaceable biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The importance of biodiversity in forests is why when I amended the Wild Animals and Birds Act through a Private Member's Bill last year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We included a new section 10 that empowers the Director-General, Wildlife Management to "issue directions to developers to carry out wildlife-related measures to safeguard wildlife, public health or safety, or the health of the eco-system." This was meant to give our Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) reports more teeth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also allows wildlife-related conditions in our EIA reports to be formally issued as directions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, we are setting up the new Khatib Bongsu Nature Park and the Sungei Buloh Nature Park Network.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have brought many people, young and old to explore Khatib Bongsu in the past few months and they are all in awe of the amazing biodiversity we have in Singapore and the need to conserve the precious green spaces we have left.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just last Saturday, my GRC colleague, Mr Derrick Goh and I kayaked with students from Secondary schools in Nee Soon to explore Khatib Bongsu.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The kids are now brainstorming and coming up with ideas on how to build this new nature park.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is more we can do to protect our flora and fauna.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It starts by not destroying the natural habitat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these species have inhabited this land long before us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They remind Singaporeans that a world exists beyond the containers of steel, glass and concrete that we live in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We call it nature, but it is also identity and it is also heritage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it will take hundreds, if not thousands, of years before a living, breathing eco-system like a forest regrows itself.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us also commit to protecting a million existing trees in our existing forests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Rachel Ong will share more of her thoughts on this topic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza will also discuss this in his speech in his Adjournment Motion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This, by the former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, "We are the last generation that can take steps to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Future generations will judge us harshly if we fail to uphold our moral and historical responsibilities." Sir, way back in 1956, the New York Times published an article, titled "Warmer climate on the earth may be due to more carbon dioxide in the air".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was a warning about climate change and how human actions will contribute to it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I live this moment in sadness and optimism.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sadness because we are somehow fighting the same battle that our forefathers fought decades ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, also optimism – because we are now much clearer about what we can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Optimism because Singaporeans, more than ever before, are speaking up and taking action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are building solar panels on our flats, reservoirs, ports and even airbases to increase our use of renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are making aggressive plans to replace conventional vehicles with EVs and hybrids to cut transport emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are facilitating green loans and green bonds to help green businesses grow.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are making big bets on carbon capture, hydrogen and other aspects of climate science as part of a massive $25 billion research blueprint.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us deepen and accelerate our climate change efforts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us slash our emissions while building new industries and creating new jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I listened to His Royal Highness Prince William as he delivered a passionate speech that has stuck with me all these years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He shared about how he had just returned from a visit to Namibia, Tanzania and Kenya, and how some of the rhinos he saw were under such threat that they had more bodyguards than he had.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "It is heart-breaking to think that by the time my children George, Charlotte and Louis are in their 20s, elephants, rhinos and tigers might well be extinct in the wild.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I, for one, am not willing to look my children in the eye and say that we were the generation that let this happen on our watch." In the same vein, Sir, let us not also in our twilight years, have to look our children in the eye and tell them we saw climate change coming and did not do all that we could to avert this climate crisis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our Government will continue working with the private sector, with our activists, and with all Singaporeans to do it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am confident that by working together, we will win this battle against climate change.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I want to thank Mr Louis Ng for raising this Motion as I believe it to be particularly important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has long been renowned globally for being a City in a Garden and that status allows us to play our small part on the world stage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, Singapore played an instrumental role behind the scenes in the build-up to the signing of the Paris Agreement in December 2015.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan played a major role in that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This was recognised by then President of the United States Barack Obama when Prime Minister Lee made a State Visit to Washington DC in 2016.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, we are known for our efforts in promoting regional sustainability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, in partnership with other countries in Southeast Asia, we can strive towards regional sustainability that protects not only our own forests, but the forests of surrounding countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can do our part, our small part to arrest climate change.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To realise this vision, we must think out of our island-box when it comes to climate change impact and possibilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of approaching this as a dichotomy between conservation and development, we must become a biophilic country that views its forests as assets to not only protect, but to grow and invest in for its biodiversity value to our residents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On that note, I would like to have it stated on record that I believe HDB and MND have already started to embody this concept of biophilia that has led to reports like the Environmental Baseline Studies, for which I am appreciative.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second point I want to make is about how we can continue to develop ground-up initiatives to cultivate a culture of biophilia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By this, I mean that sustainability should not be just a conversation or creed, but sustainability by deed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In everyday living, residents should be reducing, reusing, recycling and even upcycling.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my ward in 2019, we held a series of events at Old Holland neighbourhood aimed at reducing the use of plastics, especially single-use plastics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All the residents were encouraged to bring their own water bottles and no disposable cutlery was used at the event.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are many other avenues and initiatives aimed at reducing use of plastic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bring Your Own or BYO Singapore movement encourages consumers to bring their own reusable bags, bottles and containers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With Dover Forest, Clementi Forest and the Rail Corridor all within the area, these ecological assets have produced great biodiversity value to Ulu Pandan residents, especially during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During these past few months, when everyone had to work from home and stay indoors a lot more, many people felt a nature deficit for a prolonged period which led to greater appreciation of our forests and parks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am very appreciative of that and I will go into more detail in my Motion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, residents pointed out how they appreciated the privilege of being able to enjoy the forest alongside the various plant and animal species that reside in there.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Residents even sent me pictures of migratory eagles, allegedly from Russia and Japan who had sought shelter in Dover Forest during the wintry season.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we intensify the use of our land to fit our growing population, it is similarly important to continue providing access to nature for our residents so as to counter a nature deficit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will not only create a link between the estates along Sixth Avenue and Greenleaf to Sunset Way, but allow the residents in this area to have a convenient way into Clementi Forest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are working with SFA and HDB to explore the possibilities of urban farming sites.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A commercial operator would run the farm, but allow the community to be a part of it as we revamp community gardens to include growing more edible vegetables, fruits through hydroponics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For a low-lying island nation like ours, climate change is an existential threat.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the local scale, these changes will cause significant problems for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The magnitude of these impacts will depend on how global emissions evolve, the influence of regional factors, and, ultimately, whether we can rise to the challenge of doing our part to mitigate and adapt to climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On this note, with your permission Mr Speaker, Sir, I beg leave to introduce an amendment to the Motion before the House.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can proceed with your speech first while we check your amendments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As we have heard from the Members who have brought the Motion to the House today, so far, I am hopeful that there is common understanding of the seriousness of the threats posed by climate change on both sides of this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Declaring a climate emergency on top of the original Motion will send a clear signal to Singaporeans and the world that our nation is committed to seriously addressing one of the most long-term threats we face in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For Singapore, two consequences of climate change stand out.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The first is an increase in how variable and unpredictable our weather may become.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Singaporeans will remember very well the period of intense rainfall we experienced in the first half of January this year, the second wettest January since records began in 1869.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: While it would be incorrect to assume that these downpours were direct evidence of climate change, the increased frequency of intense rainfall may emerge as a very real consequence of a changing climate in Singapore over longer scales of time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Thus, what happened in January may have been a foreshadowing of future costs we will have to bear – the cost of floods, of mudslides and landslides, and of potholes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: These costs, in both monetary terms and in terms of the cost to human safety, will add up over the decades.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Simultaneously, we are also warned that droughts may become more frequent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: What could this mean for our water security as the supplies of water from our local catchments as well as from catchments which supply our imported water decrease?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Another consequence of climate change for Singapore is, of course, sea level rise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, there is still uncertainty regarding this figure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is why we need to continue investing in research to better project sea level rise in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We should also think about the kind of planning principles we should aim for in adapting to sea level rise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As we consider different options such as the building of extensive polders as well as other coastal management measures such as nature-based solutions, we must seriously consider all options on the table together with all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In my supplementary Budget Debate speech in October 2020, I said that, even as the Government tackle the effects of COVID on our economy, we must concurrently work on our efforts to address the climate emergency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I took the opportunity to ask the Government for an update on our efforts since the Unity Budget, and for an assurance that Singapore is on track to meet our goals and timelines for the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Today, I would like to repeat my call to the Government to provide the House with an update on our efforts to curb greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I would also like to ask how we are working with other countries, especially our ASEAN neighbours, to curb global emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: With major investments in adaptation strategies forthcoming and because the full force of climate change has not been felt by Singaporeans yet and may thus seem intangible today, it will be important to foster public buy-in and support for these efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Hence, before it is too late for the world to limit warming to 1.5-degree Celsius and for us in Singapore to plan our adaptation strategies robustly, a crucial first step is to recognise climate change as the emergency that it is.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I hope Members will agree with me that this is an important step by which the Motion today can be strengthened.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: While declaring a climate emergency will send a clear collective signal, it is not enough.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The impacts of climate change are complicated and will be felt across our country, by our biodiversity and by our people too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: People of all socio-economic backgrounds, including those who may find some policy adjustments more difficult to cope with than others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It is for this reason that we need to work together with multiple stakeholders to chart the future of our sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This brings me to the second part of the amendment we are proposing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The Motion introduced by the respective PAP Members today calls on the Government to work with the private sector and the people of Singapore to respond to climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The pivotal role that civil society stakeholders such as academics and NGOs have played and will continue to play in guiding our response to climate change cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: To illustrate this point and to argue for how we need to truly embrace sustainability in Singapore, I wish to draw the House’s attention to the example of the conservation of our forested areas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Forested spaces play a critical role in our response to climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Their vegetation and sediments act as carbon sinks, thus helping to mitigate a rise in greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: They also help to cool our urban environment – meaning a decrease in forest cover will worsen the urban heat island effect in various parts of our city-state, thereby adding to the threat of rising temperatures due to climate change on our future urban liveability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We know that forests play these important roles thanks to research by academics in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Of recent interest has been the zoning of two secondary forests – Clementi Forest and Dover Forest – for residential development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The benefits of developing housing are obvious, and these benefits are ones that we should not write off in principle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But we must also commit to seriously assessing the cost of clearing our natural capital.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: While it may be tempting to think of planting new trees elsewhere to mitigate these losses, we must remember that we are talking about the loss of benefits derived from centuries if not millennia of carbon accumulation and decades of forest regrowth which make it possible for forests to carry out the functions I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This natural heritage is one that we relinquish at our peril.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: That we even have some of these green spaces left is due to our vibrant civil society consisting of academics, NGOs such as the Nature Society and passionate individuals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: They are surveyors of our eco-systems and stewards of our environment, many of whom engage in public education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It is due to their decades of commitment – not without significant pushback from the state in the past – that we have such areas as Sungei Buloh and Chek Jawa intact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Today, our diverse community of academics and activists, both seasoned and young, have given us a better understanding of the value of many other areas including Clementi and Dover Forests.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Thus, I hope the House will support our amendment to recognise the role of these civil society stakeholders who must remain key partners in the Government’s efforts to address climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Even as the Government continues to engage various stakeholders, not least because of the large degree of influence the State has on land use planning, the onus is on the Government to better protect green spaces in the fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But if we continue to operate with the assumption that we can always free up more forests or indeed coastal eco-systems for infrastructural development, we will run the risk of relying on a land use planning paradigm that is far more inefficient and short-sighted than the Government may wish to recognise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I wish to propose the following steps we can take to better plan our land use with the aim of sustainably developing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This can be done relatively cheaply with the use of high-resolution satellite imagery and geographical information systems (GIS).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: To do this, environmental impact assessments should be conducted in a more transparent manner, engaging multiple stakeholders, including the public, during the process.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement on this?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the words proposed to be inserted, be there inserted." Mr Seah Kian Peng.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: All of us acting in concert, with resolution and most importantly, with wide agreement on the sorts of policy and behaviour that we must all adopt.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As we have seen in the current pandemic, even in matters of life and death there is sometimes room for non-compliance, for ways to "get around", learning how to bend, if not break the rules.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Public health is a funny creature of collective action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It requires all of us to play our part and together we benefit.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is vulnerable too – if the few do not comply, the many suffer.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And because it is a matter of health, we sometimes pay the highest price.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And yet – people disregard this cost – because they think they are not the ones to pay it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Because of this lack of direct link between the cause of harm and the final person who bears the burden, public health outcomes require strong regulatory intervention and social pressures.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The environment is another peculiar sort of creature of collective action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is what we would call a "common pool resource" – a sort of thing which everyone extracts benefits from, with almost no cost, but whose value is degraded with each use.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Unlike a pandemic, however, this creature is even more vulnerable because its voice is very, very soft.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The price too is high but paid in generations, so each one does not think of the final tally.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The harm too is great, but borne uneven – so that even as some die because of air pollution, others live in air-conditioned comfort.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Climate change is an important and significant issue confronting Singapore today, and it has become trite to use the word "existential" when it comes to the narrative in this House.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Everything – because we are small – becomes a matter of life and death.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Each Minister and each Member of Parliament, in our wards and constituencies, we have natural and understandable instincts to speak loudest, and feel strongest, about our own place and cause.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But as a country, we must decide as a whole, what things are most important.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The message was simple and clear; everyone has a part to play in protecting Singapore from internal and external threats.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Up till 2019, Total Defence comprised five pillars.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And so, today, our six pillars of Total Defence are: military, civil, economic, social, digital and psychological defence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Psychological Defence refers to our mind – each person's commitment to and confidence in the nation's future.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Social Defence to our links with each other – in harmony and with a strong idea of our common interests.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Economic Defence is about jobs – Government, business and industry working all working together for joint prosperity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Digital Defence, Civil Defence and Military Defence are three rings of national security, making sure all of us are defending our key interests in cyberspace, in emergencies and in times of war.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I supported this call during last year's Committee of Supply debate and continue to support it because I believe that it is an important step in Singapore's fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are three reasons: the first, because it is like all six other pillars; the second and third reasons, because it is so different.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, it is quite clear that Prime Minister already then identified it as a climate emergency.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Unlike threats such as terrorism, war and the current pandemic, climate change and environmental disasters do not have high salience.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, these issues face a perfect storm – low salience, high blame avoidance and very little chance for credit claiming.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In addition, each person would feel that his own effort would probably not move the needle.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, many Singaporeans do not have climate change in the foreground issue and do not incorporate Climate Defence in their psyche.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Placing climate change as a seventh pillar will give it priority and urgency.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a pillar of Total Defence, Climate Defence will be placed on the same pedestal as other threats.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This sends a clear message to all Singaporeans about the importance of tackling climate change and how it should be a priority.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More importantly, it underscores how a whole-of-society approach is needed to combat climate change and this leads me to the second significance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another reason again, one which distinguishes climate change from other pillars – is that it is not defence against any specific threat such as a malicious foreign actors, economic crises or cyber attackers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Rather, it is a defence against inexorable, environmental degradation that we can all play a part to fix.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Climate change, like other threats, will affect all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the good news is that everyone can also do their part to combat it, instead of solely relying on the Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While seemingly small, individual actions can add to substantial contributions towards Singapore's fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Reducing individual consumption and wastage is one such way.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We can all make a conscious effort to reduce food waste as well as our plastic waste, of which the latter is unfortunately experiencing an increase, in my opinion, because of COVID-19 and shift towards e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Individuals are in a position to also set their own environmental targets and evaluate their lifestyles to see if they have achieved what they set out to do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As what Mr Louis Ng had said earlier, as a signatory to the Paris Climate Agreement, Singapore has demonstrated that despite being a small country, it has an interest in combating climate change and is very much committed to doing so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A common perception amongst many people is that Singapore is a small country and any action taken will not have a significant effect on climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But, if every country thinks this way, then nothing will be done.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Just as important is that these policies and strategies must be communicated well to the public.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That would mean a targeted approach to communications, with usage of different mediums and content for different age demographics.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There should also be a focus on education as a way to facilitate and inculcate long-term behavioural change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The emphasis should be on promoting sustainable behaviour, particularly with regards to the 3Rs – Reduce, Reuse and Recycle.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The notion of environmental stewardship should also be underscored where we have a responsibility to the next generation to leave them a society that is better than the one we inherited.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This can be done by fostering in our young ones a connection with the natural environment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This Motion proposed by Mr Louis Ng has already consulted, in the course of the year, several groups of people – different parts of the civil society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I would also greatly like to acknowledge the good work that Mr Louis Ng and his team have put in.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need every one of us to do so too.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is one of the signatories to the Paris Agreement on climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For the first time, all nations will combat climate change as a common cause.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, even with such a landmark agreement in place, global efforts to slow down the rate of global warming are still uneven and inadequate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Climate change will cause droughts, global warming, resulting in the reduction of cold days and increase in heat waves and glacier meltdown.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These impacts will inevitably affect the social and economic structures across the globe.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Be that as it may, people are not motivated to address climate change consciously.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Climate change involves circumstances that make it hard for people to be persuaded as there are short-term benefits to both individuals and corporations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Adjustments are the hardest trade-off for people to make.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is not difficult to tell someone that climate change is affecting the world, but it is expectedly difficult to make changes when it affects an individual's habitual lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It requires a mindset change and everyone taking ownership.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should always try to replace our daily activities with greener alternatives, even if that means some inconveniences to reduce consumption.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is about every individual taking concrete steps towards the 3Rs – reduce, re-use and recycle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In Sembawang West, my volunteers and I have started a community programme to encourage our residents to embrace sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The programme includes recycling initiatives for the community and distribution of rescued fruits and vegetables to low-income families.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We hope to increase awareness, change mindset and motivate residents to adopt green habits through these ground-up efforts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over time, we have to be as green as the Scandinavian countries where an environmentally friendly lifestyle is already deeply ingrained throughout the Nordic societies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I agree with Mr Tan that the green activists and the civil society have played an important role in pushing the efforts to combat climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In fact, in the last one-and-a-half years, the YP has been involving many green activists and groups from the civil society in their public consultation work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many of the proposals and views were included in the YP paper entitled "Singapore; the Green Hub" and including the point on improving carbon efficiency.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us talk a little about improving carbon efficiency.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I was surprised to discover that concrete using Portland-based cement releases almost a tonne of carbon dioxide for every tonne of cement produced.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Concrete is widely used in the construction process.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: By weight, it is used more widely than steel, wood, plastics and aluminum combined.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, 82% of our land is used for built-up areas, for residential and commercial buildings and for public infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Given the fact that most of our buildings are high-rise, the concrete usage density is extremely high.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, how can we reduce carbon footprint in our new buildings?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am an employee of Changi Airport Group and involved in the planning for development projects, including Terminal 4 and Terminal 5.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My own experience in the built environment started almost a decade ago in 2012 when I was responsible for the closing and demolition of the Budget Terminal in Changi Airport, to make way for Terminal 4.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We moved re-useable furniture and equipment, including transporting the rooftop solar-panel, to the other terminals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The demolition contractor then salvaged the building materials, such as steel parts and concrete, and traded in these materials in the recycled materials market.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the end, we even managed to recover some cost after paying off the demolition expenses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: From there, we went on to design and build Terminal 4.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the process, I learnt about the BCA Green Mark Scheme.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We incorporated many green and eco-friendly features which earned Terminal 4 a BCA Green Mark Gold Plus Award.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The BCA Green Mark Scheme was launched in January 2005.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This green building rating system provides a comprehensive framework for assessing the overall environmental performance of new and existing buildings to promote sustainable design and best practices in construction and operations in buildings.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Green Mark scheme rates buildings according to five key criteria – energy efficiency, water efficiency, environmental protection, indoor environment quality and other green and innovative features that contribute to better building performance.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is time to make some changes to the BCA Green Mark Scheme.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One, to review construction regulations and standards, the Green Mark Scheme must encourage more use of recycled "green concrete", "pre-cast concrete and low-carbon concrete".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Green Mark can better achieve its goal of encouraging carbon-efficient construction by ensuring the Concrete Usage Index as a mandatory criterion.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For existing buildings to be greener, projects undergoing addition and alteration ought to account for lower concrete usage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Designers and owners can consider the use of sustainable materials from carbon-aware manufacturers and vendors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This proportion should be raised to encourage more recycling.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And recycled concrete can also be brought back to construction site for non-structural use.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Two, adopt environmentally friendly design approaches, materials and technologies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should allocate a higher score for the adoption of environmentally friendly designs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With creative designs, technological innovation and advancements in material engineering, such green buildings will be more common in the future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: A prominent example would be the NUS School of Design and Engineering Blk 4,or commonly known as SDE4.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Two key features of SDE4 are a large overhanging roof which hosts more than 1,200 photovoltaic panels to harness solar energy to meet the energy demands of the building and also an innovative hybrid cooling system to effectively manage the building's energy consumption by supplying 100% fresh pre-cooled air, albeit at higher temperatures and humidity levels than in a conventional system.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Other examples of successful green concepts encapsulated in the building designs include CapitaGreen, Park Royal on Pickering, Oasia Hotel, Kampung Admiralty, Bukit Canberra and Woodlands Healthcare Campus, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Three, introduce an incentive system to offset the higher construction costs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The billion-dollar question is: who should be paying for higher building costs of environmentally friendly buildings?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Most billion and multi-millionaires developers will ask: what incentives will I get to accelerate change?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They will claim that they do not directly benefit from the lower carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But the fact is whether you are a developer or a potential property buyer, you must be informed that if our environment is ever destroyed, no one escapes this catastrophe.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We cannot continue to shape policies and develop our country with a narrow view that is heavily weighed on cost and benefit analysis.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The higher costs incurred today is a worthwhile investment to safeguard our future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As a signatory to the Paris Agreement, whether it is the Government or the private sector, everyone must be prepared to go green.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I agree that the Government will have to take the lead by reviewing the current incentive and tax system in the building industry in order to encourage the private sector to play its part.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This collection could offset the higher costs for green buildings.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And on the supply side, if the demand for eco-friendly building materials, furniture and engineering systems increase, the unit cost will drop over time.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And with this new equilibrium, the market will then be able to support itself with higher demand and lower cost.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We can then discontinue the carbon efficiency grant over time.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They are non-exhaustive and I hope the key industry stakeholders, such as Singapore Green Building Council, architecture firms and construction firms will continue to work together to refine the Green Mark Scheme and make it compulsory for all new developments.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Green Mark Scheme can be our identity to embrace sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope BCA and the Singapore Green Building Council, who are co-leading the creation of the next Singapore Green Building Masterplan would consider the proposals I mentioned.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Everyone must do his or her part to expedite and deepen efforts against climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The future will always be uncertain but we must face the uncertainty of the future head-on by not being selfish and making a change in our attitudes today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just recently, at the Climate Ambition Summit 2020, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged all governments to declare a state of climate emergency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our Government has also acknowledged the threat of climate change and put in place a number of strategies to tackle this global issue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But are we doing enough as a nation?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are we acknowledging the climate emergency for what it is?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we previously committed to reduce our Emissions Intensity levels on a per dollar of GDP basis, the new NDC adopts an absolute emissions target instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a step forward as it provides greater transparency and reinforces the Government’s commitment to tackling climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, when we take a closer look at the updated target, how much has actually changed?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first NDC, submitted in 2015, stated our intention to reduce emissions intensity by 36% from 2005 levels by 2030, and this will imply emissions at around 65 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) with the aim of peaking around 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To put it bluntly, the updated target does not genuinely limit emissions growth today beyond what was already committed to under our first NDC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that the Government is targeting 33 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050, which is half that of the 65 million tonnes around 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a nation, Singapore’s climate targets still fall short of IPCC’s recommendations to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the European Union, Japan and the Republic of Korea have pledged carbon neutrality by 2050, along with more than 110 other countries.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even China, the world’s largest emitter of carbon dioxide, is pledging to reach carbon neutrality by 2060.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as a small island-state, Singapore has always been daring in our vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, I would like to propose four specific areas for improvement to reflect our nation’s commitment to tackling climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that there are significant challenges to deploying solar on a large scale in Singapore, including land constraints and local weather conditions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, we were still able to punctually achieve our 2020 solar deployment target of 350 megawatt-peak in the first quarter of 2020, reaching 1.5 gigawatt-peak by 2025 and at least 2 gigawatt-peak by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Solar, however, is only expected to contribute 3% of our electricity needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are we genuinely pushing the boundaries, or simply setting benchmarks we can easily hit?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Earlier, in January this year, I asked the Minister for Trade and Industry on whether we have a target mix for the amount of electricity generated from renewable energy sources in 2030 and 2050, and if we would consider setting a target mix that we can strive for together as a nation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I do not recall such a target being shared.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers’ Party previously called for a minimum of 10% of Singapore’s energy to come from renewable resources by 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The IEA also estimates that 30% of electricity generation globally in 2020 is already from renewable sources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A starting point for us then is having a target in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To put it simply, the IMF has described carbon pricing as the “single most powerful” way to combat climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is commendable that Singapore implemented a carbon tax in 2019, the first nation in Southeast Asia to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the current rate of $5/tCO2e, however, is too nominal, sitting far below global scientific recommendations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I fully recognise that this is a sensitive period to be raising the carbon tax and also note the Government’s plans to review the tax rate by 2023, and increase it to between $10/tCO2e and $15/tCO2e by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Member Louis Ng said earlier in his speech, this is far too low.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Government to adopt a carbon price trajectory that is better aligned with the latest research on what is effective.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It should also be complemented by financial assistance schemes to help cushion the impact of the carbon tax for lower income households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, Singapore’s refining and petrochemical sector remains an elephant in the room in our discussions on climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2017, about 75% of our industrial emissions were from this sector.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is, therefore, an urgent need to consider the role such industries will play in the Singapore economy of 2050 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Already, we are starting to see key players restructure and pivot towards cleaner energy sources, particularly in the wake of COVID-19's impact on energy demand and prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Both Shell and BP have set ambitious targets of becoming a net-zero emissions company by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Shell is investing in more lower carbon technology while expanding its renewable energy and power division.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thus far, the Government has been advocating for a practical approach, a realistic approach towards the petrochemical industry, given that it is a key employer and a key contributor to our economy today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, we are already seeing signs of the practical changes oil majors are making today, in preparing for their companies’ realistic future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given Singapore’s position as a leading oil and gas hub in Asia, it is inevitable that such changes will impact our economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, should our focus still remain on the old economy industries of the past?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With oil majors pivoting away from fossil fuels, should Singapore not proactively engage these companies, to partner them on their journey to a net-zero future?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How can we accelerate the restructuring of our economy to be better prepared for a low-carbon future which is fast approaching?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my fourth and final point, on Singapore’s potential to successfully drive the green revolution, if we genuinely commit to accelerating our efforts on this front.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not the first time we are breaking new ground for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Shell built an oil refinery on Pulau Bukom in 1961 and it was the first foreign investor to receive Singapore’s Pioneer Certificate Number 1 for its investment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A small island to the south of Singapore became one of the largest refinery complexes globally and sparked the start of Singapore’s pursuit of the petrochemicals industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the sun is setting for fossil fuels, the time has come for a new period of rapid development in the clean energy industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister Masagos previously said in 2018 that the clean energy industry will add as many as 2.2 million jobs in Southeast Asia by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking at global trends, this number will only continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To keep pace, we must continue to upsize the green industry and ensure our workforce is prepared to take on these new roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I highly commend the recent move to boost training and recruitment of local talents in the solar industries, and urge the relevant agencies to expand and extend this commitment to other green industries as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):    Mr Speaker, even as a small island-state, Singapore has always been daring in our vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Upon the 5th anniversary of the Paris Agreement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged all governments to declare a state of climate emergency until carbon neutrality is achieved at the Climate Ambition Summit 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should not only acknowledge this state of climate emergency, we can, should, and must do more.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, I would like to propose four specific areas for improvement to reflect our nation’s commitment to tackling climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers’ Party previously called for a minimum of 10% Singapore’s energy to come from renewable resources by 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Government to adopt a carbon price trajectory that is better aligned with the latest research on what is effective.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This should also be complemented by financial assistance schemes to help cushion the impact of the carbon tax for lower income households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, when it comes to Singapore’s specific measures in tackling climate change, the refining and petrochemical sector remains an elephant in the room.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is therefore an urgent need to consider the role such industries will play in the Singapore economy of 2050 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How can we accelerate the restructuring of our economy to be better prepared for a low-carbon future, which is fast approaching?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, to keep pace, we must continue to upsize the green industry and ensure our workforce is prepared to take on these new roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than seeing this as an obstacle to economic growth and progress, instead, it should be viewed as an investment into future developments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Building a zero-carbon economy is a critical pathway to more resilient economic growth in the long run – a fact that is increasingly recognised by governments and corporations around the world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Temasek, for instance, has committed to delivering a net-zero emissions portfolio by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a nation, let us challenge ourselves to push the boundaries further, to set the bar higher for the sake of our children, and to be more courageous in our collective fight against the threat of climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in conclusion, Singapore still has much room for improvement in our efforts to tackle climate change and the very first step is to recognise the climate emergency for what it is today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the beauty of it is that these changes need not come at the expense of economic growth and progress, but should instead be viewed as an investment into the industries of the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The UK’s Climate Change Committee has concluded that despite there being an overall cost in bringing about the technologies to reduce carbon emissions, there is an increase in economic prosperity in terms of an aggregate increase in GDP, jobs and real disposable incomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Building a zero-carbon economy is a critical pathway to more resilient economic growth in the long run – a fact that is increasingly recognised by governments and corporations around the world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even Temasek, for instance, has committed to delivering a net-zero emissions portfolio by 2050.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I would just like to ask Member Mr Louis Chua two supplementary questions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First of all, it is on carbon tax.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
