text: I appreciate his point about the current tax level being low and we should raise it further.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I would just like to know if he has specific targets or specific carbon tax that he thinks the Workers' Party would like to propose.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Number two, he has drawn comparison with Japan, Korea and China, which have announced carbon-neutral targets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I will leave it to my colleague, Jamus, who will be speaking a bit further on what we do propose to be the levels of the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: On the second question in terms of what some of these other developed countries have done that we have not already done, I think this is a continuum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: To me, the very first step is, as I have mentioned in my speech, that we have to set ourselves a bold target.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If you just look at the energy mix, for example, I think that is one starting point which we could consider to reduce our reliance on, basically, fossil fuel sources for energy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think that is one way where we can start to set the target for what is the level of energy generation from renewable sources that we would like to consider.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This is something which we have to start with the end goal in mind in terms of potentially reaching net-zero much earlier rather than later.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The reason for me to ask the clarification in the first place is in order to understand if that proposal to be like Japan, Korea and China has been formed with the national context, our local Singapore context, in mind, because, like all countries, we have our own constraints.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have our own opportunities to move towards renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it is important that, when we set policies and when we advocate targets here, even as we want to be ambitious, even if we want to be pathfinding, it is important to have that understanding and that realisation behind.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, that is the purpose of my clarification.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Louis Chua, do you want to respond?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But is there more that we could do to basically bring this number higher?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the past year, we had talked about children born last year as "Coronials" and "Quaranteens".

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But other than COVID-19, a longer term issue which also has implications on survival and economic viability that is top of mind for many in my generation is climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, we know that climate change is more expansive than the environment and is entangled in our socio-economic system at large; it is not a single-issue concern.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Finding and implementing solutions to climate change involve complex trade-offs, and the world we live in today has entrenched barriers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The trans-boundary nature of climate change also requires global action.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And if we truly want to move the needle, we need to strengthen cooperation across countries and move together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social norms will not change on their own.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to engage more heavily in climate change education.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to give people enough information to make informed decisions grounded in data.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate change solutions should be developed in a consultative manner, utilising nature-based solutions where possible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is nimble and can set an example, playing our part in the global community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, I am grateful for the opportunity to add my voice in support of the Motion today.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In focus-group discussions run by the Young PAP, participants expressed hopes that climate change and sustainability can be better interwoven into our national curriculum.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While geography and science subjects do touch on these topics, the teaching can be piecemeal with little being said about the social justice element and economic impact of climate change in subjects, such as Social Studies or Character and Citizenship Education.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not all our students are equally equipped to discuss these issues and they continue to see people around them leading highly unsustainable lifestyles despite what they learn in textbooks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider, first, to review the curriculum with sustainability as one of the core pillars of educational outcomes and, second, building responsible habits through a holistic approach so that it goes beyond a subject to a lifestyle?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, in "A" Level economics, carbon policies can be discussed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the "O" Level Social Studies syllabus discusses a globalised world, but its key concepts and content sections do not meaningfully incorporate climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the classroom, I am sure many of us remember the Young Scientist badges in Primary school.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent times, the community behind the Singapore Blue Plan 2018 suggested the Young Marine Biologist Badge, and Temasek Foundation and the Science Centre of Singapore have also organised the Young Sustainability Champion Programme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our efforts in educating students about climate change must include hands-on approaches such as these.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, more Values in Action projects can be jointly organised with community groups and civil society, such as Green Nudge, Zero Waste SG or the Forest School, so that students are empowered to contribute to the community and also get involved in systemic climate solutions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education and career guidance counsellors can more actively introduce pathways related to climate solutions, such as sustainable finance or engineering in green technology.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A whole-of-school approach would also be necessary, for example, the displaying of each cohort's trash to show the impact of their habits, or having a farm-to-table canteen.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that our students and our schools already run a variety of programmes, and our teachers and students have packed schedules.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate change education is also an opportunity for schools to deepen partnerships with other organisations in the community, such as interest groups and advocates, who can come in to supplement climate change curriculum, and teachers and students can learn alongside each other together, leaning on green experts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the reasons why environmental issues can feel foreign to us is because of its perceived intangibility.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, utilities bills and the My Carbon Footprint function by the SP Group are designed to help residential consumers better track and reduce their energy and water consumption, as well as their carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It provides a comparison to the average consumption of neighbours in similar housing types within a block or a street in relation to landed homes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The publishing and accessibility of such information breaks down the information in a relatable and personal way for individuals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate change solutions come not just from the Government, but also through public efforts, and I hope that more individuals take steps to actively understand their carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In driving corporate change, while previous suggestions to publish data have been met with responses that emissions data is confidential, could an alternative be to recognise and affirm low-emitters across different industries to incentivise positive behaviour?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Research has shown that younger buyers are more discerning consumers and Millennials and Generation Z have the spending power to influence the retail landscape through their purchasing decisions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Collective behavioural change can, ultimately, influence commercial decisions, and a generation of educated consumers can only make conscious consumption choices if they have the relevant information at hand.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If protected, sustainably managed and restored, nature has the power to do even more.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):    As a green and blue spaces enthusiast, I am saddened to see the change in the ocean's temperature which has affected several species of ocean life and caused the bleaching of coral reefs which previously filled the ocean with colour.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must raise awareness about the threat of climate change and how we, as a society, can take proactive steps to fight it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must explore nature-based solutions and invite the public to participate to fight climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, studies have shown that mangroves and sea grass meadows are able to store more carbon dioxide per hectare than any other forest types.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government can explore such solutions and engage more members of our community to raise awareness and fight climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker Sir, as a diver who loves our oceans, I have felt first-hand the difference in temperature in the water, seen certain species in areas where they should not be, and stared in dismay at white lifeless corals which were once alive with colour, when diving in the same place over the years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate change means warming oceans and rising sea levels, which poses a threat to reefs and marine life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond just the hard engineering of polders and seawalls, mangroves, sea grass meadows and corals can also be part of our defences against climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nature-based solutions also allow for more participatory development.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more Singaporeans are interested in the conservation of our blue and green spaces over the years, such consultative efforts, although requiring more coordination, will allow for wider public participation, so that more have a stake in our development, and better awareness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appreciate the multiple voices, both within and outside the House, on this important topic and hope that more will come forward with concrete proposals and solutions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In preparation for today's speech, I have engaged in a series of dialogue sessions, both formal and informal ones, involving Young PAP activists, climate change advocates, green-living community leaders and my Woodgrove residents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to take this opportunity to thank them for their active participation and their enthusiasm in advocating for a greener society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In these dialogue sessions, a common theme was identified, which was similar to what Members of this House who have spoken ahead of me, have shared in this House, being the recognition of that climate change is a pressing issue.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have all in some way began to feel the impact it has caused to our environment in recent years, and there is a need for us to play a part in combating climate change.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While acknowledging the issue is a hopeful first step, the question remains: have we done enough?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is easy to say, "We can and we must do more." But, are we simply just expecting to rely on our Government to roll out more policies and initiatives, while trusting business organisations to do their part in reducing carbon emissions?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The purpose of my PAP Member of Parliament colleagues who have put up this Motion today with me is that we are looking upon to explore what are the actual actions taken into account and local context that we can do bearing in mind the importance of three-piece collaborations together to combat climate change as a nation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mission, where the "G" pertains to "Green Living Initiatives".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We believe that as a community, we can do our part to combat climate change, beginning with a re-examination of our current lifestyle habits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many residents have remarked that there is a need to increase awareness and the keenness to go green, as the present efforts in our day-to-day water, waste and energy saving actions are somewhat lacking due to the lack of understanding and the passion for doing so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Meant for depositing recyclable items such as cardboards and bottles and glasses, they are more often than not, misused as common rubbish bins instead, usually due to the convenience of irresponsible dumping or a lack of proper recycling knowledge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All you need is one person to discard items containing food residue in them to cause the entire contents of the blue recycle bins to be contaminated and wastefully discarded.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I must also emphasise that in order to make this a reality, as what I have emphasised earlier, we should collectively and continuously involve the efforts of our 3Ps: People, Private and Public sectors.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In other words, this will require close mutual co-operation between the Government, Organisations and the Community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Organisations would of course include corporates, companies, VWOs and NGOs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the Government and private sectors can instate sweeping policies and provide the expertise or financial means to promote sustainability, the community also plays a vital role by getting together and through ground-up initiatives, encourage one another at a grassroots level.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The dialogue sessions that I have held with my residents in Woodgrove have left me optimistic and inspired for our future, as I discovered that many of them are willing to step up and offer their ideas to promote this cause.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, a number of my Woodgrove residents like Mr Foo and Mdm SS, have commented that while they can understand why plastic bags may still be essential in Singapore – for example, for disposing of food waste through the garbage chute – they are convinced that Singaporeans can be encouraged to develop a habit of using their own reusable bags for shopping and refusing to take more plastic bags more than they need.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under this initiative, we can collect rusted and abandoned bicycles lying around in the void decks of the neighbourhood, and send them to the repair centre for refurbishment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Once restored, they can be donated to needy children within our community for their further use.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another of the more innovative suggestions I had received revolved around the use of technology to encourage habits that promote sustainable living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Wilson, another of my Woodgrove resident, shared that the Health 365 app has proven to be popular amongst him and his peers in promoting healthy lifestyle, encouraging more people to stay active through recording progression and reward-based incentives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such activities like these will enable more residents to become the Green Advocates of our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The initiatives that we execute as a Community to raise more awareness on environmental issues will not be complete without the support of our Government agencies and private organisations as well as our community partners, like the schools which Ms Nadia has shared earlier.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We look forward to remaining engaged with them and to deepening our ties together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has proven to the world that our Government and people are willing to work together and make sweeping changes for the benefit of our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most recently, we can see that from our way in combatting the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am confident that we can harness the same strength and unity to build a green community and lead the fight against climate change for the better well-being of our future generations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Mandarin, please, for my conclusion, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):    Mr Speaker, overall, I will use the three Chinese character 加 to describe how Woodgrove is going to contribute to the fight against climate change.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we encourage more residents in participating community programmes and do their part to protect the environment, we also understand that without the concerted support of Government agencies, the private sector and community partners, our efforts to fight against climate change will not be complete.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, we must continue to invite them to participate in our community activities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, our Government and people have worked together very closely for the well-being of our people.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How we have worked together to fight COVID-19 is a case in point.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am confident that by harnessing the same strength and unity, we can fight against climate change and give our next generation a better and greener future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the growing environmental awareness and advocacy among Singaporeans have not gone unnoticed, it is especially our youths in Singapore and also around the world who have been speaking up tirelessly through movements such as Straw Free Singapore, Bring Your Own Bottle Singapore, SG Climate Rally and many more, in the struggle to institutionalise greater environmental protections – a struggle that they should not have to do alone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My generation was lucky to grow up playing in "longkangs" or drains, climbing trees and catching grasshoppers in natural environments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The access to natural eco-systems, flora and fauna had a very positive physical and psychological impact on our development.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Research worldwide has shown a strong link between green space availability, and physical and mental health.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, nature provides much intrinsic and spiritual value.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The declining opportunities for human-nature interactions has been termed by conservationists as the "extinction of experience".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The absence of such opportunities today in Singapore bears testament to the cost of solely focusing on economic development and treating GDP growth as the sole indicator of social progress.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The recent public discourse on the Ulu Pandan and Clementi forests confirmed again our Government's growth priorities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government continues to zone Clementi forest for future housing needs while Ulu Pandan forest may be slated for deforestation and development sooner.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many other forest patches have already been cleared in recent years, such as in Tengah and Pasir Ris.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order to maintain growth, we need to increase our population size and we need to clear our forests as a result to house the growing population.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We act as if the deforestation of our precious natural green spaces is an inevitability when we actually have other options.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has engineered high population growth by allowing a high level of immigration over the past two decades.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a compounded average annual growth of 1.7% which is in line with that of many developing countries facing population pressures now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This population policy is a conscious choice of the Government and is not necessarily supported by most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even assuming no increase in the non-resident foreigner population, the 55,000 new citizens and PRs will increase our population by about 0.8% a year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I pause at this juncture to note that population growth is actually not the main driver of the immediate demand for land to build housing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Housing demand depends on the Government policies in the property market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We all know that housing demand in Singapore is largely driven by investment and speculation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the result of the many conscious policies of the Government to create a sustained increase in housing prices so that the HDB flat is an appreciating asset and the buoyant property market can contribute to economic growth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While a steady rise in property values is generally good for the economy, we have also created too much housing demand.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans understandably want to leave the wage-earning class and join the property-owning capitalist class to make passive income, and developers would like to have more land to satisfy that demand.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of this, there is a huge demand for housing from foreign investors who do not even stay in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we continue to try to satisfy the strong investment demand for housing as a means to drive economic growth, we will definitely need to remove more of our green spaces.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we need to ask ourselves: is this truly what we want?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So long as each Singaporean family has a decent place to call home, should we not restrain housing demand?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, evidence is mounting that the current property policies are affecting the future of our younger Singaporeans negatively.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The long-term repercussions of having less green spaces in Singapore would affect them even more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not be sustainable to allow property prices and property demand to continue to go up at the current rate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before we rush to cut down more of our forests, we should do a comprehensive review of what is a sustainable economy and society to us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has made great strides in economic growth since Independence, moving from Third World to First.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have also experienced massive changes during the recent pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a good time for us to sit down and think carefully about the future direction of our country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we want to build a compassionate and sustainable society, or do we want to continue bulldozing through with our current unsustainable strategy of growing through immigration and property value increases?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any discussion on sustainability in our country necessarily entails a discussion in our population growth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we want to still pursue high population growth at the cost of our environment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should therefore be in no hurry to destroy our forests.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Slower population growth offers us a better foundation to pursue our sustainability agenda meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On that note, I thank the hon Members of the GPC for Sustainability and the Environment for their Motion and the 10 proposals that they have put up, which I am broadly in agreement with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there should be mention as to how these piecemeal proposals can be integrated into a future socio-economic development roadmap.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under Proposal 3, creating a sustainability sector is good in encouraging professionalism.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must bear in mind that we do not want a lot of auditors and consultants running around, who will just impose a lot of additional costs and pressures on other industry sectors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This sustainability sector should be about technology and not regulation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not want to be a climate change technology consumer all the time but the transformation roadmap must make us a technology leader.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To that end, I would like to know how the sustainability sector will create more opportunities for our SMEs and more jobs for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also unclear as to how carbon neutral or reducing some of the proposals are.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Proposal 6 on electric cars, for example, has it been conclusively proven that they will be carbon neutral under our fossil fuel energy infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there a change in our country's energy strategy?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the 10 proposals are intended to enable us to achieve more than what we have committed at the Paris Climate Agreement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another feature of the 10 proposals is that they are all climate mitigation actions and no climate adaptation actions although both mitigation and adaptation are mentioned in the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Probably as a result of that, population and forest were left out in their proposals, or at least the proposals that I have seen.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Climate Defence was mentioned in Proposal 8 but there were no proposal on how we can defend ourselves against climate change.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Adapting to climate change will require many natural and man-made solutions, the so-called "green and grey solutions", such as protecting and restoring forests and wetlands to reduce heat and flooding risks, as well as building physical infrastructure, such as dykes to prevent sea level rise and canals to mitigate flooding.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having a smaller population and retaining a larger reserve of undeveloped land can better help us to implement these solutions when the need arises.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be the true spirit for including Climate Defence into our Total Defence, not just lip service or for education purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a necessity for human survival and the flourishing of societies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is strong expectation that sustainability should embody all the human aspirations that the market system cannot effectively deliver.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sustainability has grown out of the painful experience that an economic development comes with a heavy social cost when the scale of environmental damage caused by pollution became a huge problem in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I was studying in Japan in the 1980s, there were still many victims of the "itai itai" disease inflicted by chemical pollution in Japan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And today, sustainability is not just about localised problems but have become a global crisis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With that knowledge, allowing the market system to dictate our path towards sustainable progress is unwise and will have dire long-term consequences.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the same way, we should not allow the market system to dictate the degree of social inequality in our society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We note also that as of December 2020, at least 38 countries have already declared a state of climate emergency and it is time that Singapore should take resolute action as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):    Mr Speaker, I would like to raise some clarifications to Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, from which report did he learn that our projected population would be about 10 million?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third...Sorry, I have just these two questions to ask.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In Mandarin):    I thank Member Mr Don Wee for the questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Much of our natural greenery has been lost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is why we should try to preserve our natural greenery.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, this is a figure which I have deduced based on our population growth rate.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: As a Member of Parliament, we have met many young residents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: They tell me that they have been waiting for a long time after applying for a BTO.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: According to Mr Leong’s reply, does it mean that the HDB should build less HDB flats, therefore, we do not have to cut down more trees?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The land is already there, and even if you cut down the trees now, they will not turn into BTO flats immediately.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It has been growing in urgency for some time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres highlighted the severity of the problem during the Climate and Vision Summit in December 2020.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He called on all leaders worldwide to declare a state of climate emergency in their countries until carbon neutrality is reached, noting that some 38 countries have already done so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a tropical island state, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and changes in weather patterns resulting from climate change.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the way our economy is intertwined with the global economy, disruptions resulting from climate change in other parts of the world could well have a deleterious effect on our country as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is thus important for Parliament to acknowledge that our country is in a climate emergency in order to further focus our national priorities on mitigating and adapting to climate change.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The on-going COVID-19 pandemic has hit the global economy hard.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the crisis has also provided an opportunity for us to reshape our fractured economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have a chance to develop industrial sectors, which are less destructive to the environment and thus enhance our overall resilience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We can rebuild our economy to be greener by introducing and improving measures such as one, the provision of grants, loans and tax relief directed towards green transport, the circular economy and clean energy research; two, financial support to households and businesses for energy efficiency improvements and renewable energy installations; and three, new funding and programmes to create jobs and stimulate economic activity in green industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are other steps that we can take towards reshaping our economy in this fashion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can we be more ambitious and bring forward our timeline to 2030?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Norway is aiming to reach this milestone by 2025 and the UK and Germany have aimed to do so by 2030.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, Norway is very much on track to do so and it has just become the first country in the world where electric car sales outstripped those powered by other means.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our 10-year COE system makes it easier than in most countries to have a fully electric automobile fleet earlier.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the last few weeks, we have seen an outpouring of support for the conservation of Clementi and Ulu Pandan Forests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Rather than using our limited remaining forests for urban development, we should look first into redeveloping existing industrial land and golf courses instead.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our workers are the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is crucial that we find ways to leverage on our manpower resources to develop a talent pipeline for the green economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The hard reality is many industries, particularly those in the fossil fuel-related sectors, will be hard hit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Keppel Offshore and Marine recently announced that it will be pivoting away from its offshore rig business to clean energy, in large part, due to depressed global oil demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More than 10,000 workers will be impacted by this move and it remains unclear how many will end up losing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The International Labour Organisation in its guidelines for a just transition towards environmentally sustainable economies and societies recommended several active labour market policies such as: one, helping enterprises and workers transition to the green economy by facilitating access to jobs, employment and training; two, giving particular attention to workers at risk of unemployment in industries affected by climate change including those in the informal economy; and three, introducing well-targeted subsidies that allow workers to acquire skills through work experience and on-the-job training.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In this vein, I propose extending the Special Employment Credit Scheme to provide time-limited wage support to all Singaporean workers while taking up their first job in the green economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will incentivise companies to expand their ventures in the green economy and hire and train workers in this growing industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In order to formulate more effective policies, it is important that we improve the quality and quantity of statistical data on the green economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such data is necessary for us to assess the impact of climate-related policies on our economy, health and social inclusion so that we can fine tune and adjust them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government should take the lead in promoting more sustainable practices through green public purchasing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One of the ways we can do so is by making sustainability a criterion in more public sector procurements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will provide industry with incentives to develop environmentally friendly works, products and services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It could also lead to savings in public expenditure, especially if full-life cycle costs of contracts and not just the purchase price are considered during the procurement process.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Enhancing GPP practices will also equip public officers with more knowledge and experience to meet evolving environmental challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: GPP in Singapore has already been introduced via the public sector taking the lead in environmental sustainability initiative.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Under this initiative, public sector agencies have been encouraged to put in place environmental sustainability measures, like energy efficiency, water efficiency and recycling.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Other green factors that can be considered in public procurement could include recycling, reducing single-use plastics, data centre efficiency and reduction of food wastage in catering.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is increased demand for corporate performance metrics on a range of environmental, social and governance issues or ESG as more investors seek to align their stock holdings with their issue interests and values.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the biggest survey of its kind ever done, the UN Development Programme's People's Climate Vote found that more than 60% of 1.2 million respondents aged between 18 and 59 see the climate situation as urgent, with 58% of those above 60 affirming.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We can thus expect more investors placing environmental issues as a priority.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Exchange introduced sustainability reporting in 2016 for listed companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This complements existing reporting requirements and shows the risk posed by ESG factors managed for future returns.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, no such requirement is placed on private companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government could also provide grants to incentivise SMEs to optionally submit sustainability reports.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will aid our local firms in their ventures overseas, where they may face increasingly stringent demands for sustainable business contracts, and help them to be more globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should equip our local firms before they are affected by such de facto barriers to trade.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is vital that we look into improving our energy efficiency towards reducing our consumption of fossil fuels and emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's total registered power generation capacity was 12,582 megawatts in 2020 while the highest peak system demand since 2005 has been 7,404 megawatts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This currently leaves a spare capacity of some 5,178 megawatts in the system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Combined cycle gas turbines (CCGTs) operate at a lower thermal efficiency when partially loaded.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, the Alstom GT26 gas turbine CCGT, of which there are several in Singapore plants, has a turbine efficiency of 59% at full load but suffers a 14-percentage-point drop in efficiency at a 30% part-load.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given that the power industry is the single largest source of Singapore's greenhouse gas emissions, even a small efficiency gain will reap a significant greenhouse gas abatement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on EMA data, the average thermal efficiency of power plants in Singapore in 2019 was about 50%.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can efficiency be increased by operating gas turbines at a higher average part load?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, I would like to know if EMA has looked into what impact the power generation sector's over capacity has on energy efficiency of the power generation sector in Singapore; and whether it has explored ways to increase average part loads and therefore improve the thermal efficiency of our power plants.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the deregulated market mechanisms that are currently in place, I acknowledge that this will be a challenging task.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, given the potential benefits to be gained, surely, we can find a way towards a win-win solution.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, is it possible to maintain the present deregulated system, but revert to some form of efficiency-driven-central load dispatching?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The final point I would like to make is on creating an innovation-oriented sustainability strategy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Environmental protection has traditionally been the domain of governments which set the regulatory framework and push it down to industries and households to comply.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, as Yale Environmental Studies Prof Daniel Esty pointed out in this article, "Red Lights to Green Lights", this command-and-control framework is now widely recognised as slow and inefficient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The government does most of the work of spotting problems, analysing causes of various harms, spelling out standards and requiring specific technologies to be adopted by particular industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But an over-reliance on the government as the central actor can lead to high cost, avoidable inefficiencies and disincentives for innovation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, more government incentives should be put in place to encourage broad engagement in environmental problem solving, that draws on all stakeholders, including companies, entrepreneurs, academics, civil society activists and ordinary citizens in the pursuit of a sustainable future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These practical incentives will induce innovation and help embed a green mindset in all firms and households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I suggested today some ways to enhance our efforts to integrate more environmentally friendly and sustainable practices in our firms and households.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Climate change is an issue of pressing concern in Singapore and around the world.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, we have already experienced some of the impacts of climate change in Singapore, including rising temperatures and higher rainfall intensity, which can result in flash floods, causing much disruption to our daily lives.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But what is perhaps even more worrying is that climate change can expose Singapore to potentially more serious and insidious consequences in the long run.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: For example, climate change can result in a higher frequency of extreme weather events that can affect global food production and supply which, in turn, can compromise Singapore's food security.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By diversifying Singapore's food supply sources and by ramping up our local food production, we may reduce some, but not all, of these risks .

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And therefore, one of the reasons for tackling climate change is to ensure that Singaporeans can continue to have access to quality food, that you and I, can continue to enjoy our favourite plate of Tiong Bahru "chai tow kway" whenever we want to and at affordable prices.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The climate change we are experiencing today is the result of rapidly increasing concentration of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Globally, these emissions are caused by two main activities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The first is the use of fossil fuels to generate the energy that powers our society.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The second is deforestation – the loss of our forests and natural eco-systems to agriculture, forestry, urbanisation and other land uses.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, we need energy to drive our cars, to run our businesses and to keep the lights on in our homes.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, we need land for schools, for hospitals, for housing and for the many other legitimate priorities of our society.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But, at the same time, we also need to weigh these priorities against the priority of tackling the existential threat of climate change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Achieving the Paris Climate Goal is key to reducing the risks of long-lasting and potentially irreversible climate change impacts.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And when it comes to tackling climate change, mitigation is, at least, as important as adaptation, because whereas climate change adaptation is like learning to live with the disease of climate change, mitigation is preventing or treating the disease itself, by tackling its root cause.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: First, we urgently need to reduce our emissions from the use of fossil fuels, by transitioning to renewable sources of energy, increasing our energy efficiency and cutting down on waste.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we need to protect our remaining carbon rich forests and eco-systems and avoid further emissions from deforestation.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And third, we need to start capturing and removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve these outcomes, we need to invest in the research, development and implementation of both human-engineered and nature-based climate solutions, including forest conservation and reforestation.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Achieving these outcomes also requires us to work closer together as a society.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The Taskforce is developing clear roadmaps for new growth areas and job creation opportunities, as Singapore emerges from the COVID-19 pandemic stronger, cleaner and greener.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We also have many Government-People partnerships, such as the PEERS Network, SG Cares Community Network and Youth Stewards for Nature.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Widening and deepening these partnerships may require the Government to take a more active role than before in communicating to the public, some of the thought processes and reasoning behind certain hard decisions and policies.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Nurturing such partnerships may also require the Government to be even more receptive to feedback from the public on the changing needs and priorities of society, especially with regards to climate change, nature conservation and sustainable development.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Conversely, effective partnerships may also require civil society and the public to understand the broader context of Singapore's many constraints and considerations within which hard decisions have to be made.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, as Singapore embraces sustainability in a less certain and more polarised world, it becomes ever more pressing for the Government, the corporate sector and the wider public to work together to tackle new challenges and to capitalise on emerging opportunities on the horizon.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I will be 45 this April, maybe still considered young by some Members' standards, but old enough to have been a child in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I still remember back when I was in Primary school, at Bukit Panjang Primary School.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: My parents brought me on my first overseas trip to Sydney, Australia during one of the school holidays.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: When the Australians we met heard that we were from Singapore, they spoke very highly about Singapore's reputation of being clean and green, of having the world's best airport, busiest seaport, and so on.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, I would like to speak on how we can achieve our ambitious target of peaking emissions in 2030 and then halving it by 2050.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also urge Singapore to do more, by building a carbon offset industry overseas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But to start, Mr Speaker, I would like to highlight our coming carbon emission dilemma that we, a country without much fossil fuel or renewable energy, face in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over time, as we change from cars to EVs, emissions from transport will be folded into power generation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And if, which I suspect it will, our industries continue to electrify, they will swap fossil fuel for electricity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means that over time, at the primary level, the power generation will account for the vast majority of our emissions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yet, even as we reduce the emission, we must assume electricity demand will grow as we seek to improve our people's lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, our top challenge is how to have sufficient low-carbon power generation capacity, which must supply most of our future energy needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Getting there by adapting our natural gas power generation infrastructure is not easy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Carbon and capture and sequestration techniques is too expensive in its present form for natural gas power plants, given the fact that the carbon emissions from natural gas plants are too unconcentrated to be efficient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But, yet, and that is an important point, there is an upper cap on how much we can import electricity from overseas through submarine cables if we are to maintain our energy resilience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As we speak about this issue, let us ask ourselves, can we realistically expect half of our electricity to come from overland or submarine cables?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If something goes wrong with those cables, it could take months to fix them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: What happens when we need to turn on the switch?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, our energy resilience is at stake.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, the possible low-carbon import – hydrogen, is far from ready.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It takes many years to develop hydrogen based energy infrastructure and transportation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By ready, it does not mean ready in the lab but ready in terms of infrastructure, in terms of ships that can ship liquified versions of it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, if we expect our emissions to decrease steadily immediately after 2030, in the immediate years, before affordable low-carbon power generation options are ready, low-carbon electricity will be Singapore's growth and societal constraint.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Will we see a contentious debate on who gets the first dip on scarce low-carbon electricity, much like the issue of how foreign manpower divided Singapore in the past decade?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will be facing stark trade-offs then unless everybody, Government, industry, people, civil society start moving now.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And at this juncture, let me make a broader point.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am glad to hear many inspirational speeches in this Chamber, including from Workers' Party and Progress Singapore Party.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Inspirational speeches inspire, but they are not sufficient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For something as important as climate change, we must go beyond saying "do more, do more".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Specifics matter, especially on concrete matters on that, in its entirety, can allow us to meet this ambitious targets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: What I hope is that, when we propose ideas in this Chambers, they are grounded on realities especially technological realities and informed by consultations of stakeholders from all walks of life and that we explain it to our people in plain simple terms, the trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Be it giving up on national securities when we import too much low-carbon electricity or higher cost of living or losing one's livelihood or let us say, less BTOs for young people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Only when the policy is debated and discussed in this manner, can we fully expect Singaporeans to buy in what we decide in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Now, let me next talk about how we can halve our emissions and preserve our livelihood at the same time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To achieve this, I believe we should focus on four things.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also not rush to import too much renewable electricity now, so that we at least have headroom left – by that, I mean the option of importing more renewable electricity later on – so that we can continue to improve our lives and livelihoods immediately post 2030, because of the hard limit I spoke earlier about being overly reliant on imported electricity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, I hope we can continue to invest and explore all technologies and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Government is doing a lot now including carbon mineralisation, investments in the hydrogen economy, encouraging Electric Vehicles or EVs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But the technology path ahead is not so clear for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, we should hedge our bets by exploring even unusual renewable sources, such as geothermal solutions; by exploring hydrogen based fuel cell car and biofuel options, instead of just relying purely on EVs because that would tax our electrical system and by actively investing in critical energy infrastructure ahead of time, such as, in the future, a liquified hydrogen import terminal, so that the industry has viable alternative renewable energy imports.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also be open to ideas, innovations from not just large renewable companies, but also from innovative non-incumbent players too.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And create sandboxes for new ideas to be piloted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because this is one sector where new players have consistently made an impact.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And we can weaved all this into an integrated policy and technology road map much like the visionary Reinventing Fire plans that the US and China separately did through the America's Rocky Mountain Institute.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, we can put in even more incentives beyond what we have pledged previously, to help our industries, achieve efficiency.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In particular, I hope we can come up with a determined effort to reduce emission from our petrochemical industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can also revise our Green Mark incentives, to reduce emissions for both new and existing commercial buildings.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Four, create an open and transparent process on climate change debate, as I mentioned in my opening speech in the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To Singaporeans, open and transparent process is just as important as an effective outcome.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Government can open up our plans more regularly, to share to people what we are confident to achieve and to also seek collaboration from everybody, in areas we have less confidence in achieving.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lastly, I would like to talk about how we can contribute beyond our Paris accord commitments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A number of Singaporeans and climate change believers have strongly suggested that Singapore should achieve net zero as early as possible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, I also heard some of my Parliamentary colleagues mention it today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As a Government, we are mere custodians of Singapore for future generations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We have a moral obligation to leave behind an inhabitable earth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we also have an obligation to the livelihoods of our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, let me state the obvious – Singapore is probably one of the least efficient countries to be a carbon sink.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But I strongly feel that we can do more to live up to our moral responsibility and go beyond halving our emissions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Well, as a country, we can go all out to develop carbon offsets beyond Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The means of doing so, the technology of doing so, is already there.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, can Singapore be a big player in reforesting our region, or even the rapidly diminishing Amazon rainforest?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If Singapore or our GLCs come in, in a big way, perhaps backed by MAS' green bonds, we can shape this nascent industry which currently operates without robust standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, I see much corporate demand globally, as international companies are rising to the occasion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They are wanting to go net-zero because this is what their customers and stakeholders expect.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Salesforce.com pledge to conserve or restore 100 million trees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Large companies now understand they risk being global pariahs if they do not make significant reductions, regardless of the country specific emission reduction targets in their host countries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If as a country, Singapore go big into carbon offsets through overseas reforestation, we can create value and then that could then pay for carbon offsets for the other half of the remaining emissions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some people will say that carbon offsets overseas do not accrue towards our national targets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is true, but I would say that there is nothing wrong with helping other countries meet their tough targets, especially when we all know the lack of watertight reporting under the Paris accord means that the real emission situation is probably and definitely much worse than reported as progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can complement this carbon offset industry by developing Singapore into a leading and trusted professional services hub for emissions and carbon accounting.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can encourage leading standards bodies such as the VCS and Gold Standard to set up centre of excellence to shape and promote standards, in partnership with our accounting and professional services firms as well as tertiary institutes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will create green-collared jobs that many young Singaporeans aspire for.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As we develop our carbon accounting, it is also important that we evolve the regulation of our financial markets to encourage proper disclosure and risk assessment arising from carbon emission.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Leading financial centres like Hong Kong and London are moving fast on this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, I would like to thank Mr Louis Ng and MSE's Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC), Young PAP, the VWOs and industry members I spoke to, especially people like Climate Conversations and Green Swans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a representative of a constituency with a comparatively younger demographic, many of whom are parents of young children and as a father of a young daughter myself, I have a deep enduring interest in the implications of climate change for the next generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is precisely why we should regard this issue as a climate emergency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not so much because of the specific challenges that we face today, but in terms of what we leave behind for our children tomorrow, who will bear the costs of any impending environmental disaster.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wish to commensurate with this House about the importance of a well-functioning carbon tax system for delivering effective reductions in our nation's carbon footprint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, I would argue in favour of such a tax, relative to other seemingly more efficient systems such as cap and trade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, I will also suggest reasons why the current system as it stands, is inadequate, as well as proposed some radical, some practical refinements to the existing regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, there is an existing carbon tax stipulated in the Carbon Pricing Act of 2018, which came into force in January 2019.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was an important first step as 老子 (Laozi) reminds us 千里之行,始於足下, commonly translated as "a journey of thousand miles ends with a single step." But it is only a first step and unfortunately this step has been too tentative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Systematic reviews of academic estimates suggest a price closer to $77.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our rate is even low compared to actual rates currently impose worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The OECD's calculations indicate that the effective rate among 41 major economies amount to $65.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And all these numbers are in US dollars, not even local currency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not only would this excessively conservative target fail to generate the sort of volume reductions required, it also concentrates the tax burden on a small set of firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if these firms account for the vast majority of emissions, the narrow coverage is inconsistent with public finance principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is worth noting that there an attractive alternative to the carbon tax: a cap-and-trade system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As the name implies, cap-and-trade "caps" the total amount of emissions according to some target, before subsequently allowing the trading of each firm's allocated emissions amount.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The idea behind this is straightforward: firms that are better at reducing their carbon footprints tend to gain by selling their share to other less-efficient firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, those with less carbon-reduction capacity can obtain reprieve by purchasing offsets from these more efficient firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In theory, it is possible to arrive at the same final outcome of reductions in environmentally harmful emissions with either carbon taxes or cap-and-trade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there are a number of reasons to favor taxes as a preferred instrument.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The carbon tax is more robust to uncertainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Cap-and-trade systems, while offering greater clarity over the ultimate amount of emissions that would result, tend to fall prey to uncertainty in terms of compliance costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a post-recession economic climate where uncertainty over impending costs is especially pernicious for the functioning of business, it makes more sense to allow uncertainty to fall on the total emissions front.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, carbon taxes are less likely to be gamed by participants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The experience of countries that have sought to introduce quantity restrictions on pollutants is that they are difficult to ensure compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Cap-and-trade also encourages front-loading of investments in dirty technologies, since those with greater polluting potential are more likely to be granted higher initial caps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even after implementation, permit trading can ironically encourage more pollution than otherwise, as firms trade off gains in market share against environmental penalties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In comparison, a carbon tax, based as it is on a price mechanism, is straightforward, easily observed and monitored, and hence more likely to be enforced successfully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another principle of public finance has to do with to whom the rents from the imposition of a tax or a quota accrues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because taxes are directly collected from the Government, taxes generate revenue that flow directly into the public fisc.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, if permits are simply assigned to firms, firms will capture the quota rents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not simply a theoretical matter; it also carries enormous practical implications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although the end objective – a reduction in total emissions – may be equivalently achieved via either method, carbon taxes raised can be directed toward other important social objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If instead quota permits are either simply issued or sold at an inappropriate discount to corporations, there is no guarantee that the excess value will subsequently be redirected toward the most optimal societal needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the moment, our energy and fuel sources, not to mention our export basket, remains heavily inflected toward fossil fuels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, in late October 2020, the Government announced that it would import electricity from Malaysia under a two-year trial.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I accept that part of the underlying premise for the effort is to spur a regional green electricity market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, the contours of the deal, as reported by the press, strike me as incomplete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, energy is fungible; if Malaysia sells us clean energy, only to undo our emissions gains with producing more dirty energy elsewhere, the planet will suffer as net emissions increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The deal is also symptomatic of how we tend to postpone the difficult act of passing costs through to the end consumer, some of which would ultimately be necessary to institute a behavioral shift toward a greater reliance on non-renewables.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While Minister Heng Swee Keat did announce last year that internal combustion engine vehicles would be phased out by 2040, and Minister Ong Ye Kung has stated that we could be "more ambitious" in our move to low-emissions vehicles, it is difficult to envision this occurring without a clearer commitment, at least in the medium run, toward carbon taxes applied to petrol, as well as diesel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What have we done to reduce this sector's footprint in our local economy and to transition toward more climate-friendly production?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, it is worth noting that China, despite its relatively lower per capita income, has recognised the enormous potential that green technology offers and has embraced it in earnest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It has, in doing so, taken an important lead in developing such technologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we may not have certain built-in advantages in every dimension of green tech, we could find comparative advantage in certain niche areas, as my colleague, the Member of Parliament from Aljunied Leon Perera, will share in his speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A higher carbon tax, applied more broadly across the economy, will help usher in the necessary shifts by embedding the costs of carbon emissions directly into input prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also ensures that all segments of society: business, workers, Government and civil society, internalise the costs and consequences of climate change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we wish to proceed carefully, we run the risk of our efforts being wholly unproductive altogether, if we remain excessively cautious.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In such a case, we end up with the worse of both worlds; we introduce a friction on business operation, but we fail to gain the benefits of effective climate change mitigation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another useful benchmark is $133, which is the average cost of carbon capture and sequestration activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Was this based on the latest, credible scientific evidence of the amount that would be necessary for Singapore to achieve its climate change goals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would also suggest significantly expanding the coverage of the tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has already accepted that there should be no exemptions to firms liable for the tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, it has chosen to limit the scope to the 30 or so major emitters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This runs against a standard principle of public finance, that taxes should, ideally, be small and broad, to minimise their distortionary effects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, there is little reason to retain the existing uniform tax across sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The firms currently affected by the tax are in distinct industries – petroleum, chemical, semiconductors and should the scope of coverage be further expanded, they would include firms in even more disparate sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accordingly, sector-specific taxes would offer more room to ensure that targets are met, given the varied propensity for emissions in different industries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps most crucially, the revenues from our carbon tax can then be used to offset other taxes, to ease the transition and ensure progressivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such tax-for-tax which we may call "raise and rebate" are not unprecedented, and have been exercised by the Government in the past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government can do the same this time, as a "Green Dividend".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, carbon taxes can be directed toward a "Green Fund," to be used toward investments that would further advance environmental objectives, such as solar panels or recycling operations that serve to decarbonise the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Member of Parliament for Aljunied Gerald Giam, has developed these ideas in greater detail in his speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The bottom line is that we can ensure that the tax is revenue-neutral, which can go a long way toward mitigating the negative effects of higher costs and focus instead on shifting the structure of our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, other Members of Parliament, such as Mr Don Wee and Mr Henry Kwek, have made the case for retaining the carbon tax, albeit with differing details.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, ironically, economists have moved toward this new consensus position despite being the ones to initially champion a cap-and-trade system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This shift occurred after increasing evidence emerged in favour of a tax relative to cap-and-trade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when the facts change, we should be willing to change our minds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not allow this opportunity to pass, victim to a lackadaisical policy position and undue timidity.
