speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps just as importantly, we cannot relinquish our chance to be global leaders by our signal of how a decisive move away from business-as-usual is, truly, a moral imperative.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Like all of you, sustainability is close to my heart.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It has been almost a decade since I first joined MEWR in 2011.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And in MCCY, sustainability often featured in my engagements with our youth and citizen groups.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I can speak for all of my colleagues in MSE, and across the Government, that we are encouraged by this debate, and the strong voices of support for the work that we do every day to promote a sustainable Singapore for all generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sustainability has always been a part of Singapore's DNA – always.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Even before the term became widely used, we have always pursued sustainable development by balancing economic growth with protecting our environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As early as 1967, we had the vision of a "Garden City" and took active steps to make this a reality.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The 1971 Clean Air Act, with its stringent pollution controls, is another example of our early actions to not industrialise at the expense of the environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the 1980s, we undertook the monumental task of cleaning up our rivers and made Singapore River the icon it is today.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More recently, we launched the ABC Waters programme – Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters – to realise the full potential of our water infrastructure beyond their drainage and water storage functions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Generations have transformed Singapore into the clean and green city we enjoy today.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we enjoy walks along our parks and waterways, we can take pride in the progress we have made.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With climate change looming, we will, and we must, continue to pursue this path of sustainable development.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the 2019 National Day Rally, Prime Minister Lee outlined the Government's commitment to understand, mitigate and adapt to climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Across the Government, we have charted out specific strategies to support our sustainability drive in the various sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our Energy Story aspires to transform Singapore into a bright green spark for the world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are on track to transform Singapore into a City in Nature.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are just examples of on-going efforts to energise all sectors to make climate change and sustainability core considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have been able to come this far by safeguarding not just the environment, but also ensuring economic growth and social inclusion; and galvanising Singaporeans to build a fair and just society, of hope and opportunity, that is sustainable, inclusive and resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In doing so, we have always been keenly aware of our strengths and also our constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This awareness has prompted us to tackle our challenges pragmatically and turn constraints into opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we look ahead to strengthen our national approach to climate change, it is important to recall our key immutable realities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will always be a dense and small island city-state.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have limited land, which we use to support diverse needs, including defence, industry, transport, housing and greenery.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Members noted, land use in Singapore will always be a trade-off between competing needs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Yet, we have always found a way to balance these needs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We built high-rise housing estates to house a growing population but set aside large nature reserves with about a third of the island covered by trees.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With careful planning and in pursuit of our City in Nature vision, we have been able to protect and enhance ecologically important sites as green spaces and carbon sinks over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are looking at more possibilities to enhance ecological connectivity and provide more green spaces for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, we do not have the same options for alternative energy as other larger countries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have neither great rivers for hydroelectric power, nor strong winds required for wind power.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Solar energy is our most viable renewable energy option, but even that is limited by available land area, urban shade and intermittency issues.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Mr Henry Kwek highlighted, we are taking a holistic approach to our energy challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are tapping our four energy supply "switches".

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Other than solar, we rely on natural gas, which is the cleanest burning fuel, regional power grids and low-carbon alternatives.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Other clean energy solutions may not be mature today, but show promise in contributing to our energy transformation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our research institutes are actively pursuing low-carbon energy research and development to unlock this potential over time.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, with no hinterland and no natural resources, we need a vibrant economy that is well plugged into the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will create jobs and opportunities for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To protect us from external shocks, we need a diversified economy, including maintaining manufacturing capabilities and capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is especially so in a post-COVID-19 world, where resilience, inclusiveness and reliability have become paramount.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the same time, sustainability is at the top of mind for investors and consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To remain competitive, we have to take into account these realities and balance our competing national priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It also enables many other parts of the economy, by transforming raw materials into important products that we use, including the personal protective equipment (PPE) for our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our E&C sector produces not only for Singapore, but for the world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We aim to be a responsible supplier of such products, helping our industries to shift towards lower carbon products and be among the best-in-class in energy and carbon efficiency globally.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Early on, we dared to transform Jurong Island into a world-class chemicals hub, even though we had no oil nor gas resources.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, Jurong Island is home to over a hundred global chemical firms.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The E&C sector will play a key role in the global transition to a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, the chemicals industry provides silver paste, high performance plastic films and membranes that go into photovoltaic cells and batteries for electric vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members may be aware that Neste, the largest renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel producer worldwide, will be operating its largest renewables refinery in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The E&C sector is also a key partner in the development of emerging low-carbon technologies, such as carbon capture, utilisation and storage.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These technologies can be pivotal in enabling decarbonisation at scale.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore will benefit from anchoring industry players here.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Yet, we have always tackled them squarely, turning challenges into opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This continues to hold true, as we apply the same determination to tackling climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members, like Mr Louis Ng, Ms Nadia Samdin and Prof Koh Lian Pin, have highlighted that Singapore is already feeling the impacts of climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The year 2020 was one of the top 10 warmest years on record.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Yet, June 2020 was one of the wettest and coolest Junes we have had in decades.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our weather is getting warmer, rainstorms heavier and dry spells more pronounced.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Climate change can result in more frequent episodes of extreme weather, disrupt global supply chains, encourage diseases like dengue and threaten access to food, water and energy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To effectively tackle climate change, we set up the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (IMCCC) in 2007 and the National Climate Change Secretariat in 2010.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At that time, climate negotiations were just ramping up.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We needed a whole-of-Government effort, with top-level leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The IMCCC has played a key role to oversee and coordinate both the international negotiations and domestic aspects of our climate change efforts over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, since 2007, more than 10 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And, because of this, we have a strong Climate Action Plan today.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To better understand climate change and its impact, we made early investments to boost our climate science capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will increase the scientific rigour in our policies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Launched in 2013, the Centre for Climate Research Singapore (CCRS) is now one of the few leading centres in the region, focusing on research in tropical weather and climate.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last year, we set up the Climate Science Research Programme Office under the CCRS to drive our national climate science research masterplan.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Climate change is a global challenge which will require an international solution.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: No single country will be able to tackle climate change on its own.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To mitigate the global climate threat, we need a strong global response.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All countries, big and small, must join hands to do their part.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As a responsible global citizen, Singapore, too, will play our part as part as part of a larger international solution.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is why we are a strong advocate for a robust multilateral rules-based approach to addressing climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Although we contribute to only 0.1% of global emissions, we have and we will continue to push the envelope on climate ambition, taking into account our constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have been playing an active role to sustain the momentum for global climate action, whether at the annual Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC, or by supporting fellow small states and developing countries to build capacity, implement and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are proud that experts from our Universities are making useful contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Assoc Profs Winston Chow from SMU, Lynette Cheah from SUTD and Prof Benjamin Horton from NTU are participating actively in the Sixth Assessment cycle of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore was one of the first few countries, in fact, to ratify the Paris Agreement, which enabled its early entry into force.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Members have highlighted, we do not make commitments lightly because we have every intention to make this commitment a reality.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Given our circumstances, these targets are challenging and ambitious, yet credible.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We consulted widely, and our strategies strike a careful balance between all stakeholders – individuals, businesses, green groups and academia.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many of them recognised the constraints and trade-offs that we have to work with and appreciate that we back our ambition with concrete targets and action.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will take a serious, hard look at our emissions and continue to transform our industry, economy and society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To achieve deep emissions cut, we will need to draw on technologies that are still nascent today and pursue international and regional collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have to rely heavily on cross-border collaboration, such as regional electricity grids and the establishment of a robust international carbon market with high environmental integrity.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over time, we will gain experience and better understand the extent to which potential emissions reductions can be realised.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will help us further calibrate our actions to achieve positive climate impact.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our carbon tax framework has been tailored to our context, putting in place a fair, uniform and transparent price signal to incentivise emissions reductions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We agree with Members on the importance of a strong carbon price signal in moving our industries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several Members – Mr Henry Kwek, Mr Louis Chua – provided comments on how our carbon price should be raised.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will review our carbon price by 2023, with the intent of raising the tax rate by 2030, and we note the suggestion made by Member Jamus Lim.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will take into account international climate change developments, the progress of our climate mitigation efforts and our economic competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to work closely with all relevant stakeholders to address concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Learning from our carbon tax experience so far, what had worked well for us was the clarity in our communications and close cooperation with our companies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By announcing the intent to review our tax rate early, we had provided a clear sense of direction.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This gave us and our companies the confidence and time to transit to a competitive low-carbon economy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This consultative approach must continue to feature in our work.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On our building sector, which Ms Poh Li San spoke on, we have, indeed, come a long way in our green buildings journey.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over the years, we have progressively raised our building sustainability standards and stepped up efforts to encourage the adoption of green technology and sustainable practices.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is not just in the construction process, but throughout the building lifecycle.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While we have made significant advances in the energy efficiency of our buildings, we still need building users to play their part in managing energy consumption, for example, by reducing their use of air-conditioning.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Despite our constraints as a highly urbanised tropical city, we are committed to further reducing the carbon footprint of our built environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to push for the adoption of Super Low Energy Buildings and to support the development of energy-efficient and cost-efficient green technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have been working with stakeholders on how we can achieve these aims in the next edition of the Singapore Green Building Masterplan.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mindful that we might not be able to reverse climate change completely, adaptation must also feature in our plans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We take a long-term approach to building up our climate resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: From coastal adaptation to mitigating urban heat island effects and enhancing our food supply resilience, we will plan ahead, invest in science and technology, and develop innovative solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our plans will include a combination of measures, including nature-based solutions, as Prof Koh Lian Pin has mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The benefits to such solutions are multi-fold: conserving our biodiversity and creating new recreational space for the community to enhance our living environment and, importantly, as Ms Nadia Samdin and Prof Koh have mentioned, these solutions will also contribute to mitigating climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is an exciting, growing area that we will study closely and work in partnership with our researchers, as well as international counterparts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While we have been taking serious steps through our Climate Action Plan, there is much more we can do together in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Not only will this allow us to cope with our challenges, it will provide new opportunities to test-bed and commercialise new solutions in Singapore, which may be relevant for other cities and countries facing similar challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must adopt an enabling mindset and environment, and actively engage scientists, businesses and citizens in meaningful partnerships, including civil society groups.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will keep us agile in tapping opportunities as the world transits to a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: COVID-19 has underscored the importance of transformation, resilience and cohesion in societies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore will strive to emerge stronger together from the COVID-19 crisis and build back greener and better.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are actively pursuing new opportunities, both in existing sectors and new sectors, that Singapore companies can thrive in.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will build an eco-system to support and equip our companies and people with the right skills to seize these opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, developing Singapore's capability in green financing will catalyse the growth of sustainability practices in our economy and enhance our competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Global investors are increasingly sensitised to environmental, social and governance issues, and the right allocation of capital will support sustainability projects and unlock green growth opportunities and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Mr Henry Kwek highlighted, by harnessing the potential of our carbon services industry to grow Singapore into a leading carbon trading and services hub, we can build an eco-system of expertise in this growing field.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Plastics, an issue of growing global concern, also presents an opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Just as we closed the water loop, we hope to do the same for plastics.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mechanical recycling and chemical recycling solutions can turn plastic waste into usable plastics.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are actively exploring chemical recycling that turns plastics which are not suitable for traditional mechanical recycling, including contaminated ones, into NewOil.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As part of the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 plan, we will strengthen the networks between our research institutes, and between research institutions and companies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The solutions for sustainability and climate change will come from such multi-disciplinary, yet disciplined approach to research, development and enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore is investing in public transport and is the only country in the world that has a zero-growth policy for vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will go further in making our vehicles green, including through the electrification of vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are working closely with stakeholders, including the private sector, to catalyse the adoption of electric vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will be enhancing the Public Sector Taking the Lead in Environmental Sustainability initiative so that we leverage the collective capabilities across the Government to improve resource efficiency and pursue environmental sustainability in the Public Sector.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This brings me to the importance of deepening engagements.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Louis Ng, Ms Hany Soh, Ms Nadia Samdin, Mr Seah Kian Peng brought up the need to rally everyone around the common goal of sustainable development.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And engagement not only with our community and 3P partners, across the people, public and private sectors, but also harmonious engagement with our natural environment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We strongly believe in the importance of this and have been engaging communities, schools and individuals through citizen science programmes and the One Million Trees movement, among others.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to do more, and recently launched the Youth@SGNature initiative to provide young people with more platforms to engage with nature.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Educating our young on environmental sustainability and climate change is important.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government will continue to strengthen the learning experiences for students and mould the values of our future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have heard similar hopes and aspirations, and more, at our Emerging Stronger Conversations, which many of us have been involved in, and other platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are areas of key priority to the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government has heard the voices, the suggestions and are actively incorporating these suggestions into our plans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While building on many of our past policies and programmes, we can do more to pull these different strands and efforts together, culminating in a common, united vision.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We want to rally and work with our 3P partners by articulating our priorities and goals, and we will consciously create space for the community to join hands and do more together.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ministers and political officeholders will be actively involved in the development of comprehensive programmes as part of this national engagement process.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is not just about getting feedback on Government policies, but working together to co-create solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through this process, we hope to catalyse bold, balanced and collective action.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Bold – that we push the envelope on all fronts, challenging ourselves to do more, in spite of our national circumstances and constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Balanced – for we know that, with every action and target, there are considerations and trade-offs to be made, and every Singaporean must have a voice and stake in our sustainability journey.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And collective – because we need all 3P parties, all segments of the society, to work with us to make the Green Plan a reality.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will announce more details in the coming weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister will speak about our sustainability agenda during the Budget debates.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our work to achieve sustainable development is never done.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our Singapore Green Plan will be a living document.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will adapt our plans, ambitions and policies over time.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Circumstances will change, new opportunities will emerge, and new ideas and initiatives will present themselves as we work with our citizens, businesses and communities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More importantly, we must build the social compact to deal with the challenges of climate change and sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Just as we have come together to fight the COVID-19 pandemic collectively, we will need to act with the same sense of solidarity and make collective, informed decisions on the steps we will take to achieve sustainable development as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we walk together on the sustainability journey, it is not enough for us to just set up impressive sounding goals.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will need to consider Singapore's circumstances and constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We may not be able to avail ourselves of solutions deployed in countries like China, Japan and South Korea.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These costs may manifest in the change in the price for a good or service we enjoy today, the cost of producing a product, the need to allocate scarce resources to a new solution, the investment in new infrastructure, or some inconveniences in changing our habits and the way we do things.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These costs are not a given as they can be mitigated by the choices we make.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As individuals, we can consume less, use less air-conditioning and recycle more.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As companies, we can redesign our business operations with greater efficiency in the use of resources.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And the cost differences will close over time as technology advances, as we are seeing with electric vehicles, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Hence, we need to evaluate each choice carefully, and find the right pace and balance in our policies and actions, taking into account our realities as a small city-state.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Disruptions to essential supplies, increased exposure to vector-borne diseases, and catastrophic weather.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How we view these costs and how we achieve that balance to build a sustainable future will define us and will be defined by us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The many valuable suggestions and contributions shared in this House today are very encouraging.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For some, you will be pleased to know that work is under way and you will hear more about it in the Green Plan.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For others, more time may be needed for study and review and consultation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sustainability is not just about doing more, but doing more together, in an inclusive way, with all our stakeholders on board.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I hope that Members will support us and work with us on this national movement.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is often said that the best way to predict the future is to create it.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On this note, I support the Motion, and look forward to working with all of you on this journey towards sustainability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Also, many thanks to Minister Grace Fu for sharing Singapore's multiple efforts and achievements to-date in mitigating climate change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One distinguishing mark in Singapore’s policy-making approach is our ability to think generations when designing policies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Today’s topic on deepening Singapore’s efforts against climate change is one such Think-Generations policy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The start of 2021 saw several remarkable natural phenomena in Singapore, beginning with the non-stop rain that has led to one of the highest recorded rainfall in the past 39 years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Later in the month, we then saw pink-purple algae bloom in Singapore Waterways — Mr Speaker, I am so sorry, my document has some mix-up.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Why not we move to the next speaker while you sort out your speech?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The number of speakers on this Motion from all parties in the House attests to the gravity of this issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I support the amendments proposed by the hon Member for Hougang, Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before we act, we must acknowledge the serious consequences of not acting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As Mr Dennis Tan eloquently argued, the costs of getting climate change wrong in terms of the impact on sea levels, the weather and other dimensions of the crisis are so severe as to more than warrant the term emergency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But another is the fact that this is a crisis that will deeply affect the nation as a whole and every person in it – rich and poor, fortunate and unfortunate, well-educated and not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An emergency calls for all hands on deck.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And it is in this spirit that Mr Dennis Tan’s other amendment, defining a role for civil society in our response, is important.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I argued in my maiden speech in this House in 2016, independent Singapore has traditionally had a strong state but a less strong civil society and domestic private sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this long 21st century, we need all these sectors to be strong, to contribute to diverse ideas in the public square and to augment our nation’s capacity to execute the best of those ideas, alongside a balanced political system to foster accountability, diversity of views and alternatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just as Singapore was lauded in the past for national innovations like the HDB and EDB, we can be admired and emulated in the future for mastering the intersection between economic development and environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To do this we must be ambitious, united and smart.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I will provide several examples of policies we can adopt under each of these thrusts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must go into battle with a keen sense that the costs of climate change affect people unequally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A rise in temperatures affects those who cannot afford air-conditioning more, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our climate change policies should be calibrated to reduce those inequalities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More information being made available about how well we are doing will facilitate public scrutiny and well-informed public debate about the inevitable policy trade-offs inherent in any debate on climate change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And thirdly, in terms of Singapore’s longer term green vision, our green goals should be ambitious but smart – we should aim for more green substantive targets but also ensure that our approaches add value to our economy in terms of cultivating pools of expertise, know-how, talent and entrepreneurial acumen that will drive a high-quality economy through partly exporting those skills to the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And as we battle climate change, our fight needs to be guided by a clear idea of what success looks like.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Green goals should figure strongly in the key performance indicators we adopt in Government and as a nation – not necessarily at the expense of economic indicators like household income, but alongside these.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is an important and troubling nexus between these two issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The effects of climate change would be borne disproportionately by those of lesser means – those with less resources to move house, to air-condition their homes, to filter their air and afford medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, some geographic areas are more vulnerable to these impacts than others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In responding to the climate crisis, our responses have to take into account this fact of unequal impacts and burdens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The risk is much higher for low-income residents and other people who live and work in these areas because many do not have the options for adaptation or have them to a lesser degree: no air-conditioning; shift workers who have to sleep during the hotter day-time; and older people of lesser means who are at higher risk of heat stroke.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, less living space per resident means hotter rooms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This suggests the need for progressivity in terms of our policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, can we do more to entrench innovations like anti-solar paint, especially for HDB rental blocks and HDB blocks for lower income constituents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Parliamentary colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, has made an eloquent case for an upward trajectory for the existing carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One avenue towards which the incremental revenues from a higher carbon tax could be directed would be progressively-tiered green dividends paid to Singaporeans of lesser means, to cushion the impact of the carbon tax on the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is not a new or radical idea.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Canada’s British Columbia province, the government makes payments of a Climate Action Tax Credit or BCCATC to families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The payment is quarterly and combined with the quarterly payment of other credits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I leave the issue of inequality, I would like to touch on the issue of protecting our mature forest land, but in the context of our golf clubs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our golf clubs take up 1,500 hectares of land or roughly 2% of our land area.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given the importance of protecting pristine natural habitats like mature forests, can there not be more scope to review the land devoted to golf courses as a general planning parameter, going forward, keeping in mind the fact that not everyone plays golf; the fact that there are available golfing options very close to Singapore; and the likelihood that golf is not a huge driver of inbound tourism?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the climate change cause, transparency is a critical ally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We are unlikely to achieve success in any endeavour if we do not define what success looks like and if we do not track our progress towards that end in a transparent manner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The current reporting scheme does not mandate companies to report according to specific guidelines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, reporting standards differ amongst publicly-listed companies and renders the process not very meaningful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: SGX has announced that it will improve on this front, but the improvements can and should be done in a single step with additional support given earlier on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, it would appear that environmental impact assessments or EIAs are not strictly mandatory for all major projects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, it is not clear to what extent Environmental Monitoring and Management Plans (EMMPs) have regulatory teeth behind them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There has been much mature forest that has been cleared over the years that could possibly have failed EIAs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The same can be said of Tagore forest, which was home to several endangered and threatened species.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, under the current regime, EIA consultants are hired and paid for by the developers, which can lead to a perception of conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The EMMP and EIA reports are intended to keep these same developers accountable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can an independent regulatory body administer the consultant engagement and quality controls inherent in the EIA and EMMP process?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I shall touch on how being green need not come at the expense of creating good quality jobs and an economy that delivers better quality of life for Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As as we promote sunrise future-ready green sectors in our economy and make plans to help sunset less green sectors pivot towards a greener future, we should always keep in mind the imperative to nurture domestically-rooted pools of expertise, know-how managerial and entrepreneurial talent together with the eco-system needed to root them here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can show the world how a high quality economy can be combined with sustainability just as we can show the world how it can be combined with democratic ownership and participation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is more to be done to support local entrepreneurs in fields like solar installation and maintenance, electric vehicle charging infrastructure, wind turbine construction, riding perhaps on our talent IP and know-how for oil and gas rig building, vertical urban farming, green financing and professional services for a green economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I continue, I declare my interest as the CEO of an international research consultancy that undertakes work in environmental-related sectors amongst others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But we can compete for our R&D rapid prototyping installation and maintenance activity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our companies have the opportunity to build capabilities in performing installation and maintenance in and designing products for optimised for tropical environments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Recently, Keppel started building its first offshore wind turbine installation vessel in the US which previously built sophisticated offshore rigs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need more of such examples and the Government should play a facilitating role by providing incentives support in proportion to how ambitious and capable these local firms are and how fast they can grow and create good jobs at home, in other words.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need a strongly developmental mindset and not a scheme with administration mindset.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More can be done to nurture in a very targeted manner local champions in professional services fields where there is a relative dearth of these and these fields would be, for example, clean development management advisory, carbon trading, verification, consultancy for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation in developing countries, or REDD+ and other similar consulting services.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, to make a better case for the conservation of mature forests, mangrove areas and so on, which my colleague Mr Dennis Tan spoke about and which Mr Tan and my Parliamentary colleague Ms He Ting Ru asked about in their Parliamentary Questions, can the Government commit to making sure that peripheral Woodland and green areas are accessible to the public via trails, wherever feasible?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is important to prevent mature core forests and mangroves from turning into parks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But even if they are conserved, we still need to reduce impact to sensitive areas in light of, for example, the trail erosion at Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, it is advisable to work with peripheral and non-core forests, some of which are in URA's Masterplan for development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This could yield public recreational and educational benefits which helps to cement public buy-in to green efforts as well as possibly garnering eco-tourism benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Public attention is only focused on a few of these right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The rest have also been earmarked for various land uses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can some be developed into accessible public trails that can also serve as wildlife corridors?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The example of New Zealand has attracted considerable interest globally and for good reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For years, the New Zealand government has been collecting indicators of well-being broadly defined, An OECD paper in 2019 said and I quote, "The Treasury of New Zealand has developed its living standards framework and associated dashboard to integrate well-being evidence more systematically in its advice to the government".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And, of course, this approach goes beyond green goals, but the green dimension is baked into this approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This should be accompanied with a roadmap for the decarbonisation of the public sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This roadmap should extend to all Government bodies with stronger targets or sooner targets for some rather than others, depending on their ability to cut emissions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This goes beyond what is currently being done under the Public Sector Taking the Lead in Environmental Sustainability (PSTLES) initiative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The important suggestion for green procurement by state agencies mooted by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Gerald Giam cuts along the same grain as this thrust.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also suggest that a part of our National Research Foundation funds be earmarked as a matter of policy for projects that have a high likelihood of strong environmental impact as well as tracked in terms of environmental outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These could include, for example, R&D projects related to electric vehicles, solar power and plant-based proteins.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to suggest that green goals be reflected in our Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our ITMs should have sustainability transformation goals and roadmaps baked into them as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This green dimension should not only be contained in one ITM but should be seen as a horizontal that cuts across all existing ITMs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is not only important for pursuit of our green goals, but would also help ensure the longer-term competitiveness of our ITM sectors given that environmental and sustainability standards will inevitably rise all over the world and Singapore-based companies should be ahead of the curve on this so as to stay globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I would also like to make two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, pathways into a green future should reflect transition plans for sectors and their workers that will be sunset sectors in a greener future, for example, fossil fuel industries and traditional car workshop activity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Parliamentary colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, has made an important suggestion about the use of the Special Employment Credit (SEC) to help nudge such workers to take up green jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to call for our Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWFs) to set targets to wind down their investment in fossil fuel sectors which, in any case, will face an uncertain longer term future even in commercial terms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a strategy need not be inconsistent with earning good returns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As shown by the example on performance of the Norwegian SWF, which began divesting from fossil fuels in 2019.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, can our SWFs be given a mandate to proactively invest in local firms that are developing next generation solutions for the green future in sectors like EVs, solar and plant-based proteins, for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In passing, I would like to observe that ambition plays a key role in this climate change fight.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As argued eloquently by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Louis Chua, Singapore's action is still "highly insufficient" and consistent with three to four degree Celsius warming, well below the two degrees Celsius goal targeted by the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One device to move us on the right track to is to set hard national goals for renewable energy share of total energy consumption – hard goals but realistic goals, as Mr Louis Chua argued for.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 1990, I remember astronomer Carl Sagan persuaded NASA to get the space probe Voyager 1 to turn back towards earth and take a photograph of earth before it left for the outer reaches of the solar system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The resulting photograph became known as the pale blue dot photograph which shows us the stark reality of how small this planet ultimately is in the vastness of the cosmos and how our differences as members of humanity paled beside the shared imperative of protecting the only home we have ever known.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We know the reality of the climate emergency facing Singapore in the world now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The generation that led the world through the Second World War was known in some quarters as the greatest generation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Out of the ashes of war came institutions like the United Nations, the World Bank and the IMF, that continue to play a useful role, however imperfect, in the current and hopefully soon-to-be improved world order.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Let us reflect on that for a second.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Great crises can bring out the best in us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And it is because we need to make that choice that I support the amended Motion proposed by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I had not intended to speak on the subject, but after listening to so many speakers, I am truly gratified at the support for environmental action and climate change that is coming from all sides of this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As the Chairman of the IMCCC, I have never seen such overwhelming support in so many years and I am glad that it is so forthcoming.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There has been a comment that the carbon tax in Singapore is very narrowly focused and only affects a few industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If one looks at it, you can see that we have chosen to apply the carbon tax at key nodes of carbon emissions in Singapore so that this tax will flow through evenly to the rest of the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This makes the implementation of the carbon tax and the administrative load on companies, especially SMEs, very low.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I just wanted to make this clarification so that there is no misunderstanding in this House about how we have implemented the carbon tax.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In fact, I am very gratified that many Members have made very strong arguments for a comprehensive and even carbon tax that is applied across the whole economy as a very effective way of implementing carbon emission controls.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In fact, a number of Members have advocated substantially higher carbon tax rates than we are applying today, and I hope that this will smoothen the passage of any such measures in this House when they are discussed in the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As my speech touches on carbon tax and green financing, I declare that I am working with a bank and a council member of the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The carbon tax is widely recognised as the most effective way to reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These facilities contribute to 80% of Singapore's emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In comparison, the UN's Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change recommends at least US$135.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we are looking at a huge gap here.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Proposing an increase in carbon tax during this challenging period seems counter-intuitive.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, we know that however difficult it is, we must still look beyond our immediate future to plan for decades ahead.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of the changes we need to make to combat climate change have to begin now.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, I request that these increased taxes be announced with a long period of advance notice.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the 2023 review should be the deadline by which 2030 rates are finalised.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The same review should also provide an estimate range for 2035 rates.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The advance notice is extremely important, as it gives businesses time to adapt and plan.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government should also provide the reassurance that each review of the carbon tax will take into consideration a matrix of socio-economic factors – such as projections of GDP impact, cost of living and employment – to ensure that Singapore maintains its reputation as a responsive, business-friendly hub.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The revenue from the carbon tax can be used to expand funding for energy efficiency and green financing schemes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the Energy Efficiency Fund, Resource Efficiency Grant and Genco Energy Efficiency Grant could increase their co-funding of efficiency projects beyond the current 50% for meritorious projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similar efficiency grants should also be extended to other industries, such as transportation and agriculture progressively in future, to ensure that carbon abatement is an economy-wide project.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Tax exemptions could be granted for start-ups and joint ventures that specialise in emerging green technologies and services.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government should also incentivise green financing initiatives by the banks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):    Among the climate change measures our country has implemented, the carbon tax is one of the most effective and noticeable.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although the public support environment protection measures, they are also worried about the impact of carbon tax on most consumers and small and medium size enterprises.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think that while carbon tax increases will lead to increases in utility bills, our country is still able to bear the increments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Utility bills normally only constitute a small part of an enterprise’s expenses.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After all, rental, salaries and equipment fees take up a larger proportion.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What our Government must do is to ensure that our SMEs and low-income families obtain appropriate rebates and subsidies, for example, the kueh-lapis style of tiered support to help underprivileged families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government can use the carbon tax collected to subsidise our local companies' and underprivileged families' utility bills, so that they will not be affected.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, a $5 carbon tax means a 1% increase in household's utility bills.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 has already given many of our families huge financial pressure, especially the low-income families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They face many challenges, and hence, we should reduce their burden in this area.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government had announced that the U-Save voucher scheme will be run until this year.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I suggest that the Government link U-Save with carbon tax increments, so that in this way, even when the carbon tax rises, the increase in utility rebates will be enough to offset the increases in charges.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just now, Member Mr Louis Chua suggested that the Government advocate Green Financing.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is an unprecedented scheme in the world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: GSLS will support companies to obtain green and sustainability financing, regardless of their size.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will help them to pay for the cost of hiring an independent service provider to certify the green and sustainability certificate.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The scheme also encourages the banks to introduce a loan framework to link green and sustainability, so that SMEs will find it easier to obtain this type of loan.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just now, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim quoted Laozi’s words: the journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step, I would also like to quote Laozi: Great undertakings have small beginnings, and difficult tasks are tackled from where it is easy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Minister Grace Fu mentioned just now, the Government already took the first step in 1967.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Also, many thanks to Minister Grace Fu for sharing Singapore's multiple efforts and achievements to-date in mitigating climate change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: One distinguishing mark in Singapore's policy-making approach is our ability to think generations when designing policies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: At the price of popular vote, the Government of today has often bitten the bullet, knowing that some benefits will only be reaped by our future generations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Today's topic on deepening Singapore’s efforts against climate change is one such Think-Generations policy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The trade-offs on current economic growth are real and tangible especially in light of the heavy blow the pandemic has dealt to our economy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Yet, to safeguard Singapore's long-term well-being in ways that even the deepest financial reserves cannot, we must act today.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The start of 2021 saw several remarkable natural phenomena in Singapore, beginning with the non-stop rain that led to one of the highest recorded rainfalls in the past 39 years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: We then saw mudslides and flooding in various parts of Singapore and temperatures dipped to a low of 21.1 degrees Celsius.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: These unpredictable weather patterns have increased in frequency the last decade in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Later in the month, we then saw pink-purple algae bloom in Sentosa Waterways.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The bloom is then believed to have caused the death of various fish and marine life in the waterway, a consistent consequence of similar blooms in the Mediterranean Sea.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: All the above are not isolated, curious incidents, but are sure signs of the tangible negative impact climate change has on Singapore, as pointed out by other Members earlier.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Without further intervention, Singapore may see our temperature increase from 1950s, hit 1.5 degrees Celsius within the next 20 years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Even at a previously projected population size of 6.9 million by 2030, which the Government has clarified we are unlikely to reach, we are looking at a production of 9.4 tonnes per capita of carbon dioxide, an increase rather than a decrease of where we are currently.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I urge our Government to take even more determined measures to lower our per capita carbon emissions and to do so sooner, instead of waiting till 2050 to half this target.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: To maintain global temperature rise to under 1.5 degree Celsius, every year and every decade counts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: There are two mitigating strategies to a sustainable Singapore I would like to focus on.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Second, increasing public appreciation and accessibility to nature and biodiversity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The first, reducing production of new carbon emissions; and second, removing carbon emissions in the atmosphere.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Singapore has made great efforts and progress to reduce production of new carbon emissions, an essential mitigating strategy to climate change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: They range from the Green Mark Scheme for sustainable building design, exploring renewable energy for transport and industry, extending research for new carbon capture and storage technologies, amongst many other initiatives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I also want to applaud MOT's target to switch entirely to low emissions vehicles by 2040 or earlier.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: And we should not miss out on strategies to remove carbon emissions by using natural carbon sinks that already exist in Singapore – our forests.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Forests, wetlands and soils are some of the most effective natural carbon sinks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While Singapore has made concerted efforts to retain carbon sinks in our current marine and nature conservation areas, we should leverage to our advantage the remaining forests that make up approximately 23% of our land.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Our 1 Million Trees Movement is an excellent initiative to increase our green cover and help keep temperatures cool in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: However, not all green cover is equal in their ability to sequester or absorb carbon.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Additionally, it is the production of biomass in foliage, woods, roots and the soils that store the most carbon, all of which are found in abundance in forests and limited in other urban green spaces.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Afforestation and reforestation are great measures, but retaining what forests we have, even secondary ones, and allowing them to grow to their full ecological potential will allow far more effective carbon sequestering than planting new ones.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: We can both plant new trees and retain the forested areas we have.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: We can complement our technological climate solutions with natural ones and support our remaining forests to do what they do best naturally to reduce Singapore's carbon emissions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The tension between conservation and development is real in our land-scarce nation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Yet both are now equally essential for Singapore's growth.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: For this to happen, nature must be integrated as living infrastructure vital to our development as a sustainable city state.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Singapore should continue to explore other means such as upgrading older estates, redeveloping or innovating current parcels of land for new use.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Incentives can be given for current and new infrastructure to be re-designed or designed for multiple benefits and use, such as mixes of commercial uses with community farms, community centres and schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While future generations can choose to rebuild golf courses, forests that are removed now will take decades to grow and the connected biodiversity that we lose now, may never return.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Given the forests' cumulative benefits of stabilising carbon emissions over time, we must consider our forests as our last resort.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Some may think that we are over-stating the value of forests and biodiversity to our future generations, and this brings me to my second point, that is, to increase public appreciation and accessibility to nature and biodiversity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Studies have shown a positive correlation of exposure to nature to environmentally conscious behaviour.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: However, the amount of exposure Singaporeans have to biodiversity is limited as urban dwellers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: We tend to have limited experience with nature around us beyond the roadside trees and carefully manicured parks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The impact on our population's environment comes as no surprise.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: A young volunteer at my constituency commented that his first memory of close encounters with Singapore nature was the one during his NS days and that it was not too pleasant.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Much more can be done to instill appreciation and wonder for nature within Singapore in our schools and community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Some may be aware that Singapore holds species that can only be found in our country; the Johnson's freshwater crab, which thankfully is an unlikely candidate for Chili Crab, and a Tyrannomyrmex Rex is not the dinosaur, but a rare ant species named for its resemblance to the dinosaur.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I propose two ways to raise public appreciation and accessibility to nature and bio-diversity: first, through enhanced education.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: One benefit of the pandemic has been an increased awakening to our local nature reserves and parks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: We should seize this opportunity to inform and interest our people on the bio-diversity in our midst.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: At the same time, cultivating love for nature and bio-diversity can start earlier through active education in our schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: This should go beyond the occasional excursions to nature reserves or classroom lessons, but rather, regular, immersive experiences in nature similar to the curricula we see in forest schools in Europe, US and more recently in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: An intentional and focused curricula on nature is no longer a good-to-have, but a necessity as we raise our next generation to be better stewards of our environment as Singaporeans and global citizens.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Such education should not be limited only to those who can afford private schools or enrichment programmes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: May our children's first immersion to our tropical nature not be in the form of military service, but through a growing curriculum of nature as their living classrooms.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The second way to raise public appreciation and accessibility to nature and bio-diversity is through per capita access to nature.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: It is time to review this target and clarify "green spaces" as forests, nature parks and reserves, if we are to build an urban population that is not only healthy, but also increasingly environmentally conscious.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: In light of the climate risks we now face in Singapore, I support the proposing team's proposal of the seventh pillar of Total Defence – which I had also prepared for this speech, but named it "Ecological Defence".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Singapore owns capital not limited to the human and financial.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Our natural capital, little as it may be, must be carefully invested-in even if the bulk of the benefits may only be reaped by generations to come.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I appeal to this House to accelerate investment in our natural capital by creating a conducive environment for Singaporeans and for our companies to do so.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: This will support long-term sustainability efforts in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Building a sustainable Singapore is a responsibility shared by each of us.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: As individuals, we can all do more in Singapore's fight against climate change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The recent petition for Ulu Pandan Forest has brought to national attention this needful conversation on Singapore's commitment to steward nature and fight climate change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Many residents and I are grateful for Mr Sydney Cheong, not because he started the petition but because of his genuine care for our nature, lived out day to day.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: My hope is that the conversations started will continue to extend to a larger national conversation on eco-friendly habits we intentionally adopt as individuals to make Singapore both a City in Nature and a sustainable home for all generations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):    Many of my colleagues have made suggestions to increase the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I felt a bit of unease about it, because this will increase the cost of businesses, and will, perhaps, eventually be passed on to the consumers, hence increasing their financial burden.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Any increase should be done progressively according to market needs, not at one go.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, prices will increase sharply and may cause hardship for the people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, I agree with the suggestion by some of my colleagues that the Government can use incentives to encourage businesses to reduce carbon emission, adopt alternative clean energy sources and invest in them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The relevant investment can be used to offset carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is akin to linking rising productivity with wage increases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By doing this, we can build a green economy and environment, a win-win situation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Tonight, I would like to speak on two topics: charging points for electric vehicles and the data sharing mechanisms.
