speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First of all, I would like to reaffirm my support for a car-lite Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, cars will continue to play an important role in our transport system, so we must still build an infrastructure for cars, especially electric vehicles (EV).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge the Government to ensure that sustainability will be a major consideration in the process of building charging points.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Charging point projects should only be awarded to contractors who factor in life-cycle costing and carbon footprint analysis, and provide points with energy efficiency certifications, such as those accredited by the US government with Energy Star.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At viable locations, the charging stations should be powered up by solar panels.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Users should also have the options of paying via Parking.sg app and paper coupons in the event of poor network connection or lost mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should also be able to see and compare the charging fees across different energy suppliers and charging locations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The pricing structure should use fees, demerit points and message nudges to dissuade drivers from leaving their EV at the charging lots once they complete charging.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Due to the higher costs of EVs, those in the middle and upper middle income groups are more likely to be the early adopters of EVs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Existing condos should be required to adapt existing spaces or create new spaces for charging points, with a longer grace period.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those living on landed properties, the Ministry should assist them to check and ensure that the junction boxes in their estates are able to support the charging of electric cars so that their homes do not suffer a blow-out or power trip.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government should also incentivise private developers to build publicly accessible charging points.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, with the low EV population, there is little incentive for private developers to build them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Financial incentives can be in the form of grants, tax breaks or subsidies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Public-sector data can be shared with the private sector to help them identify sources of demand, track usage patterns of Government-built charging points and disclose information on points with excessive charging demand.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will alleviate the pressure on the Government to build new charging points and also relieves congestion at the existing ones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, the Government also can look into encouraging more innovations; not just fixed charging points, but can be flexible charging points, so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This brings me to my next point on the data sharing mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All businesses recognise that pooling data, or getting access to external sources of data, can help generate value through the identification of new sources of income and cost reduction methods.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, due to reasons of confidentiality and competition, data sharing is always a challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The IMDA's Trusted Data Sharing Framework provides principles and examples that can serve as the basis of such agreements.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such a framework fosters collaboration and benefits companies in many ways.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The EU is already leading in such data-sharing systems.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Shared European Logistics Intelligent Information Space brought 37 logistics entities together to create a trusted data-sharing environment for the industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the Netherlands, the logistics and transport sector came together to develop iSHARE, a uniform set of agreements to identify and access management among organisations, allowing all parties to easily share data with business partners and downstream entities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For Singapore, several industries could do something similar.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Retail developers can share data on the reliability, efficiency and quality of common fittings, energy-saving technologies and other energy-consuming equipment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SMEs in the manufacturing sector could have a standardised digital system for reporting sustainability-related data points, which makes it easier for downstream clients to assess such data points and comply with their own sustainability requirements.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The benefits of such frameworks for climate change are significant.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to increases in efficiency and the reduction of resource consumption, such frameworks nurture the growth of specific sectors, nudge them towards digitisation and increased data sophistication.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Ministry would consider my recommendations in support of the Motion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Hence, declaring a climate emergency in Singapore alone is insufficient.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Singapore has done a fair amount of balance of growth development and environmental protection, but actions against climate change must take place in Singapore and beyond our shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Be it roadmaps, the type of investments, supply chains, energy demand and much more.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Singapore is part of a larger international solution.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thus, we need to look into these efforts globally and how they impact mankind.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Singapore can certainly contribute our part and we must do so no matter how small or large we are.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Having heard many suggestions and views from the Members on both sides of this House, we all agree that this is an area we should focus on and it is the actions and measures taken now that matter.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The efforts and commitment, however, should not be shy of determination and innovation from different stakeholders in society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Today, I will touch on two themes – the need for sustainability accounting on greenhouse gas emissions (GhG) and carbon emissions and preparing the talent pool to embark on this green economy in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It is my hope that we can achieve our goals in fighting climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Let us begin by discussing how through different aspects we can enable Singapore to be more focused in our actions and obtain more tangible outcomes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: First, greater accountability and consistent standards of measursing GhG and carbon emissions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The development of framework to deal with GhG and carbon emissions depends heavily on the ability to measure, account and document emissions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To be fair, many companies and industries have already introduced standards to measure carbon emissions as part of their Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) contributions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, the pertinent issue is, there are many different standards and accounting practices being used, thereby making it difficult to do a cross-industry assessment or benchmark companies within the same sector.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Before the proposals, I will provide an understanding of what other jurisdictions are doing globally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Regulators globally are currently adopting a more prescriptive approach to ESG reporting by making such reporting mandatory rather than voluntary.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In 2007, Sweden mandated state-owned companies to publish sustainability reports.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In June 2020, the Bank of England also published its first climate risk disclosure report based on the framework by the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, TCFT.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: More recently, regulators have begun to introduce ESG reporting obligations for financial market participants and not just companies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Europe is the first jurisdiction to mandate ESG reporting for asset managers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: From March 2021, asset managers in Europe will be required to disclose how they integrate ESG factors into their investments.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Additionally, the UN Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDG) has called for the harmonisation of accounting standards for GhG to facilitate transparency, accuracy and comparability of climate actions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thus, I would want to propose concrete actions through the following.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Using standardised reporting frameworks, which I will elaborate on later, this would help establish a common criterion of measurement and consequently assessment in the annual carbon footprint of an organisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thus, facilitating baseline comparison across different companies and industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As a next step, companies can establish carbon emission reduction targets against their baseline and the industry's benchmark of an "ideal carbon footprint".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This would better help Singapore companies take reference and adjust their goals using the industry benchmark.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In a way, companies that are ahead of the curve in their decarbonisation plans and emission measurements can share best practices with those experiencing difficulties in meeting their targets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Further, with industry-wide efforts and Government directive, the focus can be placed in dedicating resources towards assisting companies in finding ways to remedy and improve their situation rather than penalising.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It is the collaborative ecosystem approach that we want to encourage in the value chain and bring all parties towards the same goal.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thinking longer term, with a more standardised and quantified approach, we as a nation will be better positioned to continuously review the adequacy of our carbon emission target and adopt technological solutions to accelerate our achievement towards the goal.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While there are many GhG accounting standards adopted by industries today, the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) and the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) appear to have the largest relevance and ease of adoption across industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: These frameworks are also recommended by UNSDG and the market participants.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The frameworks have their respective strengths and identified subsets of ESG issues most applicable to financial performance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Additionally, it recognises that not all sustainability issues have equal weightage to each industry and the same sustainability issue may manifest differently across industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While the Singapore Exchange or SGX currently mandates ESG reporting, the reporting guidelines are loosely framed, which allows for much flexibility in reporting.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thus, hampering the ability in making meaningful interpretations and comparison of emissions that we urgently require to understand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In the interim, more can be done educating and heighten awareness amongst the local SMEs on the significance of selected frameworks' applicability to their industries and the annual ESG Reporting method.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The purpose is to gain their buy-in and not merely treating this as another regulation that needs to be adhered to or increasing cost of business.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This way, we exercise prudence to ensure that the smaller SMEs have a roadmap to adopt the frameworks and compliance cost of ESG reporting is taken into consideration for future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Next, getting everyone onboard the fight in climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The Green Economy is a new model of sustainable growth and an exciting one.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, there exists a gap today between interests of participants entering this economy and their ability to embark.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Much needs to be done to develop Singapore's infrastructure and talent pool for sustainable accounting, should it eventually become legislated and the job opportunities in Green Economy blossom.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To bridge this gap, here are some suggestions of immediate actions that can be taken to enhance the quality and understanding of sustainability for those interested to participate in this field.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: One, provide more variety in the courses at Institutes of Higher Learning for those who are interested in the field of sustainability field as a career.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: For example, financial accounting for sustainability, low carbon manufacturing and materials, food supply alternatives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Two, facilitate early or mid-career moves towards jobs focused on environmental sustainability in partnerships with companies through structured mentorship and work transition programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The industry sectors with more advance capability around sustainability can provide the inputs to our strategies and guidelines on the roadmap for others to take reference.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This hybrid approach will enable MTI to better shape the development of training, programmes and infrastructures to create more eco-friendly business environment that supports inclusion of sustainability within the sectors over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With a sustainability ITM, sustainability will be put at the forefront and elevating its role and importance within businesses and our society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The public-private sector partnerships through economies of scale can be better deployed when there is visibility and definition of scope as opportunities arise across industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Greater exchange of best practices, R&D and innovation can also be identified with greater synergy for collaborative work to drive the Green Economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Further, data pooling will ultimately result in better design of processes, improved efficacy, shorten learning curve, drive fresh investments and reduce the overall carbon footprint.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I firmly believe we can achieve the same for the sustainability industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Climate change is indeed a very existential threat to our world and our country today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The pressures will only increase as our demand for energy and as a developed economy continues.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It is essential that we cultivate civic consciousness to the extent that sustainability becomes our way of life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: So, not only do we need to get everyone on board to fight against climate change, we must lead the way and lay the foundations today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Some of the younger Members in this House will have no idea what I am talking about.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It was a cartoon series about protecting our planet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is how the opening went, "Our world is in peril.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Gaia, the spirit of the Earth, can no longer stand the terrible destruction plaguing our planet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She sends five magic rings to five special young people: Kwame, from Africa, with the power of Earth; from North America, Wheeler, with the power of Fire, from the Soviet Union – yes that is how old this cartoon is – Linka, with the power of Wind; from Asia, Gi, with the power of Water; and from South America, Ma-Ti, with the power of Heart.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: When the five powers combine, they summon Earth's greatest champion, Captain Planet." I also remember the show's catchy theme song, but I remember Speaker's Facebook post about not getting any ideas about singing in Parliament, so I shall not sing it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I also remember one sentence, something Captain Planet said over and over again: "The power is yours." As I shared in my opening speech, Singaporeans, more than ever, believe in Captain Planet's message.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They believe the power to protect the planet is theirs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But our optimism must not take us away from our urgency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We are hurtling towards extreme climate change and we must urgently change course.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government must help by deepening and accelerating our efforts against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Two, professionalise the carbon accounting and reporting industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Three, incorporate sustainability into the Industry Transformation Map scheme or have an ITM for the sustainability sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Four, enhance the Public Sector Taking the Lead in Environmental Sustainability initiative with higher and expanded standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Five, introduce rules and incentives to promote the building of publicly accessible charging points by private developers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Six, revise the Green Mark scheme to increase standards on carbon intensiveness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Eight, introduce data-sharing mechanisms on clean energy technologies and energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Nine, increase public access to emissions data of top-emitting private companies and public entities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ten, and lastly, add Climate Defence as a seventh pillar of Total Defence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These 10 recommendations will help us meet and, I believe, exceed our commitment under the Paris Climate Agreement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I will not be able to do justice to everyone's speeches but let me summarise some themes of their proposals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Members stressed the importance of protecting our natural carbon sinks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Miss Rachel Ong shared the science about trees and alerted us that keeping existing trees is far more effective than planting new ones, though both are important steps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked for additional legal protection for secondary forests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ms Nadia Samdin, Prof Koh Lian Pin and Miss Rachel Ong rightly noted that our corals, our mangroves, and indeed, our forests powerfully trap carbon and help us fight climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The three Members also stressed the importance of helping Singaporeans learn and become more in touch with nature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This brings me to the second theme: education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For them, Ms Nadia Samdin discussed installing sustainability as a core pillar of our education system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Miss Cheryl Chan suggested preparing young adults so they have the interest, skills, knowledge and connections needed for the green sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But education is not just for the young.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Christopher de Souza discussed this, his exciting vision for Ulu Pandan as a nature surplus neighbourhood, with nature trails, community gardens and food composting sites.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ms Hany Soh painted a colourful portrait of her Woodgrove community and discussed how all Singaporeans could learn about sustainability through hands-on experience and convenient technologies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The third theme for today is incentives and regulations – in other words, carrots and sticks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: All Members proposed solutions that would limit carbon intensive activities but they also made sure to suggest ways to soften the impact and spark the economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Don Wee discussed using carbon tax revenues to grow our industries and protect our households.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim similarly asked to give out a green dividend from our carbon tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested sharing Government data to help the private sector figure out where to build electric vehicle charging points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked to extend subsidies and support for petrochemical workers as the industry shrinks its global workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Leon Perera proposed growing our green industry, particularly those dealing in professional services, like environmental impact consulting and carbon trading verification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ms Poh Li San suggested a circular financing system to help the construction industry adapt to tougher Green Mark standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked for increased support and a more generous timeline for SMEs to file ESG reports.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Louis Chua asked for greater reliance on solar energy and cited statistics to show how the clean energy sector can create good jobs for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Henry Kwek pitched solutions like investments in geothermal solutions and carbon offsets to help the economy adjust to decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Together, these balanced recommendations show that Members want Singapore to be both green and prosperous, not just one or the other.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He also raised some general concerns about trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I mentioned, many Members have been proactive in raising these trade-offs in their speeches and propose specific ideas on how to overcome them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There is no disagreement that a healthy economy and a healthy environment need to go hand in hand and I encourage Mr Leong to continue sharing his ideas on how to manage these trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Leong said that forest protection and climate adaptation were not included in the Motion's 10 topics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I think Mr Leong will find that several Members today have raised proposals on both topics, myself included.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The 10 topics are not an exhaustive list.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Leong also asked whether EVs would reduce emissions in Singapore's context.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I agree with Mr Tan on the importance of civil society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I spent more than two decades of my life as a civil society activist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We have not just recognised the role of civil society but we have actively engaged them throughout the year long consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They have played a crucial role in this Motion and, as I mentioned, in my opening speech, this Motion responds to their call.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The original Motion's statement focused on the three Ps that we are all familiar with – the public, private and people sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I have shared in my opening speech, Prime Minister Lee has already stressed that climate change is "one of the gravest challenges facing humankind." This Government already recognises that the existential threat of climate change is an issue that nations cannot ignore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I believe all of us in this House are on the same page but, Sir, we drafted the Motion's statement that reflects actions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I believe this will reflect the climate change issue more holistically and focus again on action on how we all need to work together in this global community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope that all of us in this House will support the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To conclude, I would like to refer to a point Mr Seah Kian Peng made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As part of his ask to include Climate Defence as a pillar of Total Defence, he argued that Singapore needs to take bold, unprecedented steps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There must be a new willingness, a new resolution by the Government to do things differently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It will take time, but every corner of policy-making – and indeed way of life – must transform to match our aspiration towards sustainability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My heartfelt thanks also to the GPC for Sustainability and the Environment, the Young PAP's Climate Change Policy Team, my Climate Change Team, business leaders, researches, activists and fellow Singaporeans who all contributed to this Motion and the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Each one of us in this global community also plays an important role and by working together, this battle is strengthened and this fight for our planet becomes stronger.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Let us make sure that climate change becomes a thing of the past, something our children learn about in this history lessons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Let us change our mindset, our behaviours and our policies to move the needle on climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Let us focus on action and deepen and accelerate efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change, and to embrace sustainability in the development of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I open up for clarifications and comments, there is carbon footprint that comes from long sessions of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: At first glance, I have a concern that the amendment pertaining to the word "That the climate change is a global emergency" seems to have de-emphasised the importance of climate change in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But I think I do recall that Miss Chan did mention something along the lines of not just in Singapore so I believe we are in agreement that, as many Members in the House today have expressed concern of that climate change, how it affects Singapore, how it affects the world and the efforts that all of us, locally and all round the world, need to make.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, on that note, I am prepared to accept these amendments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Miss Chan also mentioned about the term "a threat to mankind".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Perhaps, it should be more appropriately worded "as a threat to humankind" or, in fact, "a threat to all life on earth".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, we have now finally come to the conclusion of the debate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I shall put the question to the House for decision.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have an amendment by Miss Cheryl Chan and two amendments proposed by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Miss Cheryl Chan's amendment is that after the word "acknowledges" in Mr Tan's first amendment to leave out the words "a climate emergency" and there to insert the words "That climate change is a global emergency and a threat to mankind".
